research:oss_solo_sustainability.dimension: How solo or part-time maintainers build successful open-source infrastructure (case-derived rules for a solo, part-time AgentOS maintainer)
research:oss_solo_sustainability.executive_summary:
GitHub API data pulled on 16 October 2026 shows that the most successful "solo" AI and OS infrastructure projects still depend heavily on their founders, even at very large scale. The founder wrote 68.6% of Open WebUI's commits (155,856 stars), 73.7% of Coolify's (63,038 stars), 68.7% of Omarchy's (44,921 stars), 66.1% of Bazzite's and 100% of Pinokio's. Gaining contributors did not lift the founder's load. llama.cpp is the one exception: Gerganov wrote 17.4% of 11,691 commits, spread across roughly 2,100 contributors, because hardware vendors and Hugging Face staff contribute backends.

Every breakout case started as a narrow wedge built on someone else's heavy lifting. llama.cpp targeted one model on one laptop ("4-bit quantization on a MacBook"), and Simon Willison had it running one day after release. Ollama wrapped llama.cpp behind a one-line curl install. Open WebUI began as a front end for Ollama. Omarchy and Universal Blue configure existing distributions: Arch, and Fedora Atomic via bootc and GitHub Actions. Asahi Linux is the counter-case because it did hardware bring-up and kernel upstreaming. Its lead resigned in February 2025, citing burnout, user entitlement and harassment, with more than 1,000 downstream patches still outstanding.

Donations do not fund an OS. Asahi's Open Collective has raised about USD 156,000 in roughly 20 months for a seven-person team, and Tidelift reports that 60% of maintainers are unpaid. Large sums came only from four sources:
- venture capital (Ollama, USD 88M)
- angel investors (ggml)
- celebrity patronage (Omarchy, USD 23.65M pledged, self-reported)
- acquisition (ggml by Hugging Face in February 2026; Astral by OpenAI in March 2026)

Public grants are small or restrictive. NLnet first grants run EUR 5,000-50,000, and its programmes are in transition. The Sovereign Tech Fund requires a scope above EUR 50,000 and excludes prototypes.

Permissive licences dominate. Open WebUI's non-OSI branding clause and Redis's SSPL episode show that restrictive licences cost trust. Jan moved from AGPL to Apache 2.0 to make adoption easier.

The founder's premise has a structural tension. A solo, part-time founder wants an operating system that is both bootable and "revolutionary," while developing on an M1 Pro that cannot test CUDA fine-tuning paths. The evidence points to a bootc image layer rather than a new distribution, one safety demo that users can verify, Apache-2.0 plus a trademark policy, and keeping a day job.

pain_points.title: Founder remains the dominant committer regardless of popularity
pain_points.description: Contributor growth does not transfer the core workload. Even projects with 44k-156k stars show the founder authoring roughly two-thirds or more of all commits, so bus factor stays near one.
pain_points.segment: Solo founders of application-layer and distro-layer open-source projects
pain_points.evidence: GitHub API, 16 Oct 2026: Open WebUI tjbck 13,393 of 19,511 commits (68.6%); Coolify andrasbacsai 13,153 of 17,846 (73.7%); Omarchy dhh 4,829 of 7,026 (68.7%); Bazzite KyleGospo 5,693 of 8,613 (66.1%); Pinokio cocktailpeanut 677 of 677 (100%). Counter-example: llama.cpp ggerganov 2,032 of 11,691 (17.4%).
pain_points.quantified_impact: Founder share 66-100% in 5 of 7 sampled successful projects; only library-layer llama.cpp diffused authorship.
pain_points.current_solutions: Hiring a first paid developer from sponsor or cloud revenue (Coolify, mid-2024); shared leadership after founder exit (Asahi seven-developer model); joining a larger company (ggml to Hugging Face).
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Opinionated products require one coherent vision; drive-by contributors fix edges, not architecture; review cost of outside PRs often exceeds writing the code.

pain_points.title: Donations are small and decay after the launch peak
pain_points.description: Community donations peak at launch and then decline, and even well-loved OS projects raise less than one Western salary per year from crowdfunding.
pain_points.segment: Bootable OS and hardware-enablement projects; volunteer maintainers
pain_points.evidence: Asahi Open Collective: USD 156,337.62 raised, estimated annual budget USD 117,653.87, for a seven-developer team (Oct 2026). Hector Martin: 'The all-time peak monthly donation volume was the very first month or two' (Feb 2025). Tidelift: 60% of maintainers are unpaid hobbyists, 12% earn most or all income from maintenance (Nov 2024).
pain_points.quantified_impact: About USD 118k per year spread across seven developers for a high-profile OS project.
pain_points.current_solutions: Fiscal hosting (Open Source Collective), GitHub Sponsors, sponsor logo tiers, corporate GPU or CI donations (LocalAI via Spectro Cloud).
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Users treat infrastructure as free; corporate users rarely pay for indirect dependencies; donation platforms offer no recurring value exchange.

pain_points.title: User entitlement, support load and issue backlog
pain_points.description: Popular projects accumulate large open-issue queues and feature demands that a part-time maintainer cannot service, which drives burnout.
pain_points.segment: Desktop and OS distributions; local-AI runners
pain_points.evidence: Open issues (GitHub API, 16 Oct 2026): Ollama 4,296; Bazzite 1,206; Pinokio 475 with a single author. Hector Martin: 'No matter how much we did... people always wanted more.'
pain_points.quantified_impact: Hundreds to thousands of open issues per project; Asahi lead resignation attributed partly to demands.
pain_points.current_solutions: Discord-based community support (Bazzite, Coolify 20k+ members), aggressive issue closing (Open WebUI shows 170 open issues against 155k stars), Discussions forums.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Hardware diversity in OS projects creates unbounded bug surface; users expect product-grade support from volunteers.

pain_points.title: Upstream friction for low-level OS work
pain_points.description: Projects that must change kernels or drivers carry large downstream patch stacks and depend on slow, sometimes hostile upstream review.
pain_points.segment: Hardware enablement and kernel-level OS projects
pain_points.evidence: Asahi downstream tree held over 1,000 Apple Silicon patches not yet upstream; M3 and M4 support deferred until upstreaming and CI progress (Feb 2025). Martin: 'Upstreaming to Linux is a terrible experience in C too.' May 2026 addendum: he will forgo participation in the community entirely.
pain_points.quantified_impact: 1,000+ patch backlog; new hardware generations blocked.
pain_points.current_solutions: Shared maintainer teams, CI on device farms, prioritising upstreaming over features.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Kernel governance is outside any single project's control; reviewer bandwidth upstream is scarce.

pain_points.title: Commercial free-riding and rebranding prompt licence changes that erode trust
pain_points.description: Companies repackage permissively licensed work without contributing, pushing maintainers toward restrictive licences that then trigger community backlash or forks.
pain_points.segment: Popular AI front-ends and infrastructure with enterprise demand
pain_points.evidence: Open WebUI added a branding clause in v0.6.6 (19 Apr 2025) because 'some groups were stripping out the branding, repackaging our work as their own, and monetizing it'; licence is not OSI-approved and post-v0.6.5 contributions require a CLA. Redis moved to SSPL in March 2024, which 'hurt our relationship with the Redis community' and led AWS and Google to maintain a fork; Redis added AGPLv3 on 1 May 2025.
pain_points.quantified_impact: Loss of OSI status; ineligibility for funds requiring OSI/FSF licences (Sovereign Tech Fund).
pain_points.current_solutions: Branding clauses, enterprise licences, SSPL/AGPL, trademark enforcement.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Permissive licences maximise adoption but permit rebranding; restrictive licences reduce adoption and contributor goodwill.

sources.title: Redis is now available under the AGPLv3 open source license

pain_points.title: Social-engineering and AI-generated noise target exhausted maintainers
pain_points.description: Overloaded maintainers are vulnerable to pressure campaigns for co-maintainer access and are increasingly swamped by low-quality AI-generated reports.
pain_points.segment: All solo maintainers, especially security-relevant system software
pain_points.evidence: xz: maintainer cited 'longterm mental health issues' and 'an unpaid hobby project' (8 Jun 2022) while likely sockpuppet accounts pressed for a co-maintainer who later gained control. curl: about 20% of 2025 security submissions AI-generated, about 5% valid, each report engaging three to four people for 30 minutes to 3 hours (14 Jul 2025).
pain_points.quantified_impact: curl security team of seven spends multi-person hours per invalid report; xz led to a backdoor in a core OS package.
pain_points.current_solutions: Bans and reputation systems, private security advisories, considering removal of bounties.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: New accounts are cheap; AI makes plausible-looking submissions nearly free to produce.

pain_points.title: Public grants are small, slow, or exclude early-stage and user-facing projects
pain_points.description: Non-dilutive public funding exists but its eligibility, size and timing rarely fit a new, solo, user-facing OS project.
pain_points.segment: Pre-traction open-source founders in or outside Europe
pain_points.evidence: Sovereign Tech Fund: minimum estimated cost above EUR 50,000, about six months to contract, 'We do not finance the development of prototypes', user-facing applications not sought. NLnet NGI Zero Commons Fund: first grants EUR 5,000-50,000; final call closed 1 Jun 2026; a 12 Jun 2026 notice says open calls temporarily paused during the transition from NGI to an Open Internet Stack; new calls listed with a 3 Nov 2026 deadline. GitHub Secure Open Source Fund: USD 10,000 per project in tranches.
pain_points.quantified_impact: Typical first grant EUR 5k-50k or USD 10k; six-month lead times.
pain_points.current_solutions: NLnet calls, GitHub Secure Open Source Fund, a16z Open Source AI Grants (2023 cohort included text-generation-webui and vLLM).
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Funders prefer reusable base technology with proven usage; programmes are cyclical and politically dependent.

pain_points.title: Trust backlash when a wrapper commercialises without crediting upstream
pain_points.description: Thin layers over other projects grow fast but face criticism over attribution, lock-in and cloud pivots once they raise venture money.
pain_points.segment: Wrapper and orchestration projects built on llama.cpp or similar engines
pain_points.evidence: Practitioner critique (15 Apr 2026) links Ollama issue #3697 (llama.cpp omitted from README for over a year), a July 2025 GUI shipped without a licence and open-sourced in November 2025 (PR #12933), and cloud models possibly forwarding prompts to third parties (issue #14279). Ollama has raised USD 88M (9 Jul 2026) and introduced per-token pricing (31 Aug 2026).
pain_points.quantified_impact: Reputational; motivates competing projects and forks.
pain_points.current_solutions: Adding upstream credit, open-sourcing components after criticism.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: VC growth incentives favour proprietary differentiation over upstream credit.

sources.title: Friends Don't Let Friends Use Ollama (practitioner opinion)

pain_points.title: Discovery is dominated by founders with existing audiences
pain_points.description: Distribution reach, not technical novelty, explains much of the gap between celebrity-led and unknown-founder projects.
pain_points.segment: Unknown solo founders launching OS or desktop projects
pain_points.evidence: Omarchy (DHH) self-reports 1,280,643 ISO downloads in year one and USD 23,650,000 pledged to the Omacom Foundation, reaching 44,921 stars in about 16 months; Pinokio, a technically ambitious solo project, has 8,260 stars after three years. llama.cpp spread via Simon Willison's write-up one day after release.
pain_points.quantified_impact: Order-of-magnitude difference in adoption between audience-backed and unknown launches.
pain_points.current_solutions: Building in public, demos, Hacker News and Reddit launches, newsletter coverage, integrations with popular tools.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Attention is concentrated; demo virality is unpredictable.

trends: Acquisition by AI labs and platforms is now a common way for successful AI-infrastructure open-source projects to end up: ggml.ai joined Hugging Face (20 Feb 2026) and Astral agreed to join OpenAI (19 Mar 2026).

'OS for agents' positioning has gone mainstream. Omarchy markets itself as 'The malleable OS for the age of agents', with default-agent setup on first boot (Oct 2026). Ollama and Fly.io promote running agents safely (13 Oct 2026).

Image-based Linux built with bootc, OCI and GitHub Actions has cut the maintenance cost of derived distributions. Universal Blue images are cosign-signed with 90-day rollback, and ublue-os/main narrowed to fewer base images in September 2025.
Local-first tools are turning to cloud revenue: Ollama cloud models (preview September 2025), per-token pricing (31 Aug 2026), and Coolify Cloud.
Licences cycle between restriction and permissiveness. Redis went to SSPL in 2024 and added AGPL in 2025. Jan moved from AGPL to Apache 2.0 in 2025. Open WebUI added a branding clause in 2025.
AI-generated reports and PRs are adding to maintainer load: about 20% of curl's 2025 security submissions were AI-generated.
European public funding for open source is in transition. The NGI Zero Commons final call closed 1 Jun 2026, open calls were paused on 12 Jun 2026, and new calls carry a 3 Nov 2026 deadline.
Corporate-patron foundations are emerging for desktop operating systems: the Omacom Foundation lists Meta Superintelligence Labs, DigitalOcean, Alibaba Cloud and others as patrons (Sep-Oct 2026).
Shared or company governance increasingly follows a founder's exit or acqui-hire: Asahi moved to seven-developer shared leadership, and ggml moved under Hugging Face with stated autonomy.

opportunities.idea: Make the AgentOS wedge an 'agent action that is always reversible': agents run in confined sandboxes on an atomic bootc base, and any system change an agent makes can be rolled back.
opportunities.why_now: Agent-first desktops such as Omarchy give agents broad control, and safety demand is visible (Ollama with Fly.io, October 2026). Atomic images already provide 90-day rollback.
opportunities.evidence: Pinokio's README admits risk when a script 'intentionally tries to deviate'. Bazzite offers rollback to any build in the last 90 days. Omarchy's agent features show no sandboxing claims on its homepage.
opportunities.risk: Universal Blue, Omarchy or Fedora could add similar features quickly. Sandboxing GPU workloads is technically hard and may be impossible to test on an M1 Pro.

opportunities.idea: Ship AgentOS as a derived bootc image (FROM a Universal Blue or Fedora bootc base) instead of a new distribution, distributed via 'bootc switch' and ISOs built by bootc-image-builder.
opportunities.why_now: The ublue-os image-template packages the build, signing and ISO pipeline in GitHub Actions.
opportunities.evidence: Universal Blue states it is a way to consume existing distributions, not a new one, and its images are built entirely by GitHub Actions with cosign signing.
opportunities.risk: Depends on upstream base-image decisions (for example, ublue-os/main reduced its images in September 2025). The product may look like 'just another spin' unless the agent layer is distinctive.

opportunities.idea: Become an integration target for existing ecosystems (the Ollama integrations list, Open WebUI, llama.cpp packaging, MCP clients).
opportunities.why_now: Hugging Face's stated post-acquisition goal is to make llama.cpp 'ubiquitous and readily available everywhere'. Ollama lists about 154 integrations.
opportunities.evidence: Open WebUI grew as a front end for Ollama. Ollama grew by wrapping llama.cpp.
opportunities.risk: Commoditisation, and the attribution backlash that Ollama experienced if upstreams are not credited.

opportunities.idea: Seek non-dilutive funding for a reusable security component (an agent sandbox or capability policy) rather than for 'the OS'.
opportunities.why_now: New NLnet calls carry a 3 Nov 2026 deadline. The GitHub Secure Open Source Fund accepts applications on a rolling basis.
opportunities.evidence: NLnet first grants are EUR 5,000-50,000. The GitHub fund gives USD 10,000. The Sovereign Tech Fund excludes prototypes and user-facing applications but funds base technologies.
opportunities.risk: Programme transitions and pauses; six-month lead times; eligibility may require residence or legal-entity conditions that remain unverified.

opportunities.idea: Later, offer a paid hosted service (remote GPU fine-tuning or fleet management) while keeping the OS fully open.
opportunities.why_now: Precedents show hosted revenue funding the free core: Coolify Cloud, and Ollama's cloud models with per-token pricing.
opportunities.evidence: Coolify funded its first hire in mid-2024 from sponsors and paid users. Ollama has raised USD 88M on a local-plus-cloud model.
opportunities.risk: Trust erosion if the cloud is pushed by default. Running GPU infrastructure is capital-intensive for a solo founder.

recommendations: Do not build a distribution. Make AgentOS a single Containerfile layered on a Fedora bootc or Universal Blue base, built and cosign-signed in GitHub Actions from the ublue-os image-template, with ISOs built by bootc-image-builder. Hold v0.1 to one repository, one image and under 1,000 lines of your own code.

Write a NON-GOALS section before the first commit, as uv did at launch: no custom kernel, no new installer, no own inference engine (use llama.cpp, Ollama or vLLM), no desktop environment work, and a single CPU architecture for v0.1.

Choose one demo users can verify and build only toward it, for example: boot from USB or switch with 'bootc switch', run an agent against a local model in a sandbox, then undo everything it changed with one rollback command. Record a video under 90 seconds. llama.cpp spread within a day because its claim was concrete and checkable.

Match targets to your test hardware. Develop and test the aarch64 image in a VM on the M1 Pro, label x86_64/NVIDIA and fine-tuning paths as community-tested, and recruit at least two hardware testers before claiming GPU fine-tuning support.

Launch on one day in sequence: Show HN, then r/LocalLLaMA, then the Universal Blue Discourse. Submit to the Ollama and Open WebUI integration lists in the same week. Before launch, publish a weekly devlog for 8 to 12 weeks to build the audience you currently lack (Omarchy's advantage is distribution, not code).
Credit every upstream prominently in the README and boot splash (llama.cpp, Fedora, Universal Blue). Ollama's attribution backlash shows the cost of not doing so.

License your own code under Apache-2.0 (with its patent grant) and accept contributions under a DCO. Protect the name with a TRADEMARK.md policy, not licence clauses. Avoid custom or non-OSI terms: Open WebUI's branding clause made it non-OSI, which would also bar Sovereign Tech Fund eligibility.
Expect to write 70% or more of commits for years, as the founders of Open WebUI, Coolify, Omarchy and Bazzite do. Budget contributor work as review and triage, not as relief.

Cap time strictly. At about 10 hours per week, allocate roughly 6 to building, 2 to docs and demos, and 2 to triage. Use issue forms that require reproduction steps, convert support questions to Discussions, and publish a policy requiring disclosure of AI-generated PRs and security reports (the curl lesson).

Harden governance against xz-style takeover. Grant commit or release rights only after six or more months of verified contribution, require two-person review for build scripts and test fixtures, and use GitHub private security advisories.

Keep your day job and treat donations as a bonus. Asahi raised about USD 156,000 in 20 months for seven people. Open GitHub Sponsors on day one, apply to NLnet's next call (3 Nov 2026 deadline, or the following odd-month deadline) for the sandbox component, and apply to the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund once you have traction.

Decide your exit stance in writing now: an independent foundation, a hosted-service company, or openness to acquisition. The 2026 acquisitions of ggml and Astral show that labs buy projects that become infrastructure, and contributors will judge you on your stated intent.
contrarian_signals: Restrictive licensing did not visibly stall Open WebUI. It reached 155,856 stars and 889 contributors by October 2026 despite its non-OSI branding clause, so the 'restrict and die' narrative is not universal.

Contributor growth did not reduce founder load in most cases. Founders still author 66-100% of commits in five of the seven sampled successful projects, so expecting the community to share the work is unsupported.

Much of the success is distribution, not technology. Omarchy's self-reported 1.28M downloads and USD 23.65M in pledges rest on DHH's existing audience, and an unknown solo founder cannot replicate that model.

The most celebrated 'solo' successes ended in venture funding or acquisition (Ollama USD 88M; ggml to Hugging Face; Astral to OpenAI), which conflicts with a purely independent, community-owned AgentOS vision.

Hardware-level OS ambition is the documented burnout path. Asahi's founder resigned in February 2025 and in May 2026 withdrew from the community entirely, which supports an image-layer approach over bespoke hardware enablement.

The 'AI-native OS' framing is already taken by a well-funded player. Omarchy calls itself 'The malleable OS for the age of agents', so 'revolutionary' must mean a specific capability, not positioning.

Grant funding is shrinking or in transition just as the founder would need it: NGI Zero Commons' final call closed in June 2026, open calls were paused, and the Sovereign Tech Fund excludes prototypes and user-facing applications.
Thin-wrapper strategies invite backlash: Ollama faced attribution, lock-in and privacy criticism, which suggests that wrapping upstream engines without visible value-add carries reputational risk.

The founder's premise contains an internal inconsistency. Fast, safe local fine-tuning on CUDA hardware cannot be developed or verified on an M1 Pro with 16 GB, and Asahi does not yet support M3/M4, so bare-metal Apple Silicon is a narrowing target.
open_questions: Methodology limit: the shared web-search budget ran out after 13 distinct searches, below the 20-search target. The remaining evidence comes from about 25 primary sources read directly and live GitHub API queries. Remaining gaps include the full Tidelift 2024 survey data, Sovereign Tech Agency Fellowship terms, Ollama's 2023 Show HN date, and the Mozilla and a16z cohorts in 2025-2026.

Clarifying question for the founder: what single capability would make AgentOS 'revolutionary' and that Omarchy, Universal Blue or Ollama could not add within six months? Without a precise answer, the bootable-OS requirement adds cost without differentiation.

Clarifying question for the founder: should fine-tuning run locally on the user's GPU, remotely, or both? The M1 Pro cannot test CUDA paths, and the answer determines whether v0.1 targets aarch64 VMs, x86_64 NVIDIA, or Apple Silicon via Asahi.

Clarifying question for the founder: is the long-term intent an independent foundation, a hosted-service company, or openness to acquisition? This determines whether to use a DCO or a CLA, and how to word governance commitments.

research:os_level_primitives.dimension: What an AI OS can do only by owning the OS layer: agent-native kernel and system primitives
research:os_level_primitives.executive_summary:
Owning the OS layer gives a real advantage, but a narrower one than the "agent kernel" papers suggest. The flagship research does not run in the kernel. AIOS (COLM 2025) and its semantic file system LSFS (ICLR 2025) run as Python userland layers. AIOS reports up to 2.1x throughput, measured on one RTX A5000, and its last tagged release is v0.2.2 from March 2025. Several other ideas also work in userland serving engines: MemGPT context paging, KV-cache virtual memory (vAttention, kvcached) and token-level GPU pooling (Aegaeon, which Alibaba says cut GPU use by 82% in a beta deployment). Today's coding-agent sandboxes (Anthropic sandbox-runtime, OpenAI Codex) already isolate commands with bubblewrap or Seatbelt without a custom OS. Anthropic reports 84% fewer permission prompts from this approach.

The OS image genuinely matters in five areas:
- **Guaranteed kernel features.** Landlock has reached ABI 11 (UDP rules, TSYNC). BPF LSM needs the lsm= boot parameter, and sched_ext and kprobe override need specific kernel config. Userland tools cannot assume these, so they fall back to weaker modes: Codex demoted Landlock to legacy, and Claude Code needs AppArmor workarounds and a weaker nested mode inside containers.
- **Covering every agent process.** Claude Code's sandbox covers shell commands only. MCP servers, hooks and LSP servers run with full access, and an unsandboxed retry exists.
- **Per-agent identity and network control.** The kernel can identify each agent and enforce its egress rules without relying on proxy environment variables.
- **System-wide undo.** A Btrfs root laid out at install time allows one-step rollback of the whole system, not just files.
- **Checkpoint/restore and patched GPU drivers.** gpu_ext, for example, needs patched NVIDIA modules on Linux 6.15.

The closest existing product is Windows' preview On-device Agent Registry. It runs MCP servers under separate agent accounts, but grants file access per host app rather than per server. No product found combines all of the following on Linux: agent identities enforced by the kernel, eBPF enforcement that knows the agent's intent, per-agent egress with credential injection, and one-command system rollback.

Hardware constraint: on the M1 Pro, the Asahi GPU driver is outside mainline Linux, the Neural Engine driver is out of tree, and all GPU-partitioning research found is NVIDIA-specific.

Method caveat: the shared web-search budget ran out after 7 searches, short of the 20 requested. The remaining evidence comes from about 32 primary sources fetched directly.

pain_points.title: Userland agent sandboxes leave much of the agent outside the boundary
pain_points.description: Current coding-agent sandboxes wrap shell commands, not the whole agent system. MCP servers, hooks, LSP servers, status-line helpers and plugin processes run with full user access. An escape hatch lets the model retry a blocked command unsandboxed, and docker is incompatible with the sandbox.
pain_points.segment: Developers running coding agents and MCP tool ecosystems on Linux and macOS workstations
pain_points.evidence: The Claude Code docs say the sandbox covers shell commands only, and that hooks and local MCP servers run with full access. The docs also describe the dangerouslyDisableSandbox retry and state that docker is incompatible with the sandbox. Anthropic's answer is to wrap the entire Claude Code process in sandbox-runtime, which is a beta research preview.
pain_points.quantified_impact: Anthropic reports that sandboxing cut permission prompts by 84%, which shows how much friction it removes for whatever it covers. No figure exists for the risk carried by the unsandboxed components.
pain_points.current_solutions: Wrapping the whole process with sandbox-runtime (srt), dev containers with firewall scripts, Docker Sandboxes microVMs, and contained MCP servers in Windows ODR (preview).
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: A userland tool can only sandbox the processes it launches. Other software starts MCP servers, IDE helpers and browsers under the user's full identity, and only the init system and kernel can apply one policy to every process an agent starts.

pain_points.title: Kernel feature fragmentation forces weaker sandboxes
pain_points.description: Agent sandboxes must run on whatever kernel and security settings the host provides, so they fall back to the weakest common mode. Codex now defaults to bubblewrap and keeps Landlock only as a legacy option. Ubuntu 24.04 blocks unprivileged user namespaces unless an AppArmor profile or sysctl change allows them. Inside unprivileged containers, bubblewrap cannot mount /proc, so Claude Code offers an explicitly weaker nested mode.
pain_points.segment: Agent tool vendors and security-conscious developers on mixed Linux distributions
pain_points.evidence: The Codex linux-sandbox README makes bubblewrap the default and marks Landlock as legacy because Landlock cannot isolate app-server Unix sockets. The OpenAI sandboxing docs and the Claude Code docs both describe the AppArmor userns restriction on Ubuntu 24.04. The kernel documentation shows Landlock at ABI 11, with UDP rules only from ABI 10, which only very recent kernels have.
pain_points.quantified_impact: No quantified impact found. The visible effect is that sandboxes skip available kernel features (Landlock UDP and TSYNC, BPF LSM) and use more privileged mechanisms such as user namespaces.
pain_points.current_solutions: bubblewrap plus seccomp, warning messages at startup, distribution-specific AppArmor profiles, and weaker fallback modes.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Tool vendors cannot control which kernel version, kernel config (CONFIG_BPF_LSM, CONFIG_SCHED_CLASS_EXT, CONFIG_BPF_KPROBE_OVERRIDE) or boot parameters (lsm=) a user has. An OS image controls all three.

pain_points.title: Network egress control is hostname-based and can be bypassed
pain_points.description: Per-agent egress control usually works through an HTTP or SOCKS proxy that checks the hostname the client supplies, without inspecting TLS. Allowing broad domains such as github.com opens exfiltration paths, and domain fronting can reach hosts outside the allowlist. Docker Sandboxes cannot chain non-HTTP TCP traffic to an upstream proxy. The Windows alpha of sandbox-runtime does not fence DNS.
pain_points.segment: Enterprises and individuals worried about prompt-injection-driven data exfiltration
pain_points.evidence: The Claude Code docs warn about domain fronting and state that TLS is not inspected by default. Docker Sandboxes' architecture page says proxy chaining applies only to HTTP and HTTPS. The srt README says DNS is not fenced on Windows.
pain_points.quantified_impact: Not quantified in the sources reviewed.
pain_points.current_solutions: Host-side proxies with domain allowlists, experimental TLS termination with credential masking, Docker Sandboxes' sentinel-credential substitution, and custom MITM proxies.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Strong per-agent egress needs four things at once: kernel-level identity for each agent (cgroup or socket hooks), transparent redirection that does not depend on proxy environment variables, DNS control, and a trusted CA installed in the system store. All four are OS-image concerns that no single tool controls.

pain_points.title: No system-wide transactional undo for agent actions
pain_points.description: When an agent breaks something, users can roll back files in a workspace, but not the system state the agent changed (installed packages, config, services). Existing options are file-only or tied to a single app.
pain_points.segment: Developers who let agents run autonomously; operators of long-running agents
pain_points.evidence: Fly.io Sprites offers whole-filesystem checkpoints in about a second, but restores roll back files only, not running processes. Turso's AgentFS (3.5k stars) offers copy-on-write isolation and SQL audit over FUSE or NFS, but is in beta. Btrfs snapshots are instant metadata copies, but they are not recursive across nested subvolumes and are not backups.
pain_points.quantified_impact: Not quantified. The demand signal is AgentFS at 3.5k stars and Sprites building its product around checkpoints.
pain_points.current_solutions: App-level checkpoints in coding agents, git, AgentFS, cloud VM snapshots (Sprites, Firecracker), and manual Btrfs or ZFS snapshots with snapper.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Atomic rollback of a workspace together with the system it changed requires choosing the filesystem and subvolume layout at install time, plus an immutable or layered root (bootc, systemd-sysext). Only the OS image can guarantee that.

pain_points.title: Tools either observe agents or enforce rules, but none links the two to intent
pain_points.description: eBPF observability tools for agents link LLM prompts to system calls but cannot block anything. eBPF enforcement tools can block actions but do not know which prompt or tool call caused them. Tetragon's SIGKILL alone does not guarantee that a write is stopped; it must be combined with return-value override.
pain_points.segment: Security teams and power users auditing autonomous agents
pain_points.evidence: AgentSight (PACMI 2025) captures TLS LLM traffic and correlates it with process and file events at under 3% overhead, but it only observes and needs root. Tetragon's docs state that SIGKILL alone may let a write complete and that Override must be added.
pain_points.quantified_impact: AgentSight reports under 3% overhead. No measurement of detection coverage was found.
pain_points.current_solutions: AgentSight, Tetragon, Falco (detection), and proxy logs.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: An intent-aware deny decision needs BPF LSM enabled at boot, kprobe override in the kernel config, and a trusted daemon linking agent identity to its LLM session. Distributions do not ship that combination by default.

pain_points.title: Sharing one GPU between interactive inference and background fine-tuning lacks OS controls
pain_points.description: Running interactive agents, model serving and training on one accelerator suffers from head-of-line blocking and weak isolation. The kernel has little GPU control: the dmem cgroup only limits device memory for TTM-based drivers (Intel xe first), and research schedulers need patched NVIDIA drivers.
pain_points.segment: Local AI developers and small labs with one or two GPUs
pain_points.evidence: LithOS reports 4.7x lower tail latency than NVIDIA MPS for mixed inference and training. gpu_ext reports up to 4.8x decode throughput but needs instrumented NVIDIA open kernel modules on Linux 6.15. The kernel cgroup-v2 docs show dmem regions only in the form drm/<PCI>/vram0 for xe.
pain_points.quantified_impact: The research claims above (13x and 4.7x tail-latency gains against MPS) imply large untapped gains, but none of it ships in products.
pain_points.current_solutions: NVIDIA MPS, MIG (datacenter GPUs), time-slicing, and userland serving tricks (kvcached, Aegaeon-style token-level preemption).
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: GPU drivers are proprietary and differ by vendor. Kernel GPU cgroups are new and partial, and the research needs custom kernels and drivers. Apple Silicon under Linux has none of these mechanisms.

pain_points.title: Checkpoint/restore of agent processes that use GPUs is partial and risky
pain_points.description: Pausing, migrating or forking a running agent along with its model state is only partly supported. NVIDIA's cuda-checkpoint does not support UVM memory. Cloning microVM snapshots duplicates randomness, tokens and identifiers unless uniqueness is enforced.
pain_points.segment: Agent platforms needing pause/resume, branching and preemption
pain_points.evidence: cuda-checkpoint integrates with CRIU 4.0+ from driver 570, adds GPU migration in 580, and does not support UVM memory. CRIUgpu (Feb 2025) claims transparent CUDA and ROCm checkpointing but gives only qualitative claims in its abstract. Firecracker's docs warn that resuming the same snapshot more than once is insecure without uniqueness handling.
pain_points.quantified_impact: Not quantified in the sources reviewed.
pain_points.current_solutions: CRIU with cuda-checkpoint, Firecracker snapshots, Sprites (files only), and app-level state serialization.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: CRIU needs kernel config and privileges, GPU support depends on the driver, and Apple and Asahi GPUs have no checkpoint path.

trends: The isolation boundary is moving to a microVM per agent: Docker Sandboxes, Apple Containerization (one VM per container), Kubernetes agent-sandbox with gVisor or Kata, Firecracker-based clouds, and libkrun on macOS.
OS vendors are adding agent identities to the OS: Windows runs MCP servers under separate agent accounts and sessions, with admin policy and audit (preview, November 2025 onward).

eBPF is becoming the policy layer for everything: sched_ext (CPU scheduling), BPF LSM (access control), gpu_ext (GPU memory and scheduling), AgentSight (agent tracing), and systemd v258's PrivateBPF and BPFDelegate options.
OS-style virtual memory for KV caches is happening in userland, not in kernels: vAttention (ASPLOS 2025), kvcached, Aegaeon token-level pooling (SOSP 2025), and Pie inferlets.

Landlock is maturing fast (ABI 11, including UDP, TSYNC, audit and IPC scoping), yet the major coding agents rely on bubblewrap because kernel versions vary across users. Owning the OS image closes that gap.
Checkpoints are becoming a product feature: Sprites (about 1 second, files only), CRIU with cuda-checkpoint, Firecracker snapshots, and AgentFS time-travel.
Wasm is becoming a capability sandbox for tools: WASI 0.3 shipped in June 2026, Microsoft Wassette runs MCP tools as Wasm components, and Pie runs Wasm inferlets.
'Agent OS' research mostly runs above the kernel (AIOS, LSFS, MemGPT, MemOS). The truly kernel-level research (gpu_ext, LithOS) targets NVIDIA datacenter workloads.
Apple Silicon Linux is stabilizing: Asahi Mesa drivers went upstream in August 2025 and M3 support arrived in September 2026, but GPU compute and the Neural Engine remain second-class.

opportunities.idea: Agent principals as a first-class OS object: every agent, tool and MCP server launches as its own systemd transient unit or cgroup, with stacked Landlock rules, a BPF LSM policy and per-agent egress identity. A user should be able to ask 'what can agent X touch?' and get a kernel-enforced answer.
opportunities.why_now: Windows shipped agent accounts and sessions in preview, which validates the concept. Linux has every needed piece (Landlock ABI 11, BPF LSM, cgroup socket hooks, systemd v258 delegation), but no distribution combines them by default. Userland sandboxes leave MCP servers and hooks unsandboxed.
opportunities.evidence: Claude Code docs (MCP servers and hooks run outside the sandbox); Windows MCP containment docs (separate agent user account); Landlock kernel docs (ABI 11); systemd v258 release notes.
opportunities.risk: Duplicates srt and bubblewrap if done shallowly. The fix is to build the policy compiler on top of srt and bwrap rather than replacing them, so the difference is OS-wide default enforcement.

opportunities.idea: Transactional agent workspaces with system-wide undo: a Btrfs subvolume per task, automatic snapshots before and after each action, an immutable root with layered extensions (bootc or systemd-sysext), and a single 'agent undo' that rolls back files, installed packages and config together.
opportunities.why_now: Agents increasingly act autonomously. Sprites and AgentFS show demand, but both work at the file or FUSE level, and only an OS that chooses the root filesystem layout at install time can include system state.
opportunities.evidence: Sprites checkpoints in about 1 second with file-only restores; AgentFS has 3.5k stars and is in beta; Btrfs snapshots are instant metadata copies.
opportunities.risk: Btrfs snapshots are not recursive and not backups. Databases and running services need quiescing. Needs careful subvolume design.

opportunities.idea: Intent-aware enforcement: combine AgentSight-style TLS and syscall correlation with BPF LSM deny decisions, so every blocked action is linked to the prompt and tool call that caused it, plus a replayable audit trail.
opportunities.why_now: AgentSight (2025) showed the correlation costs under 3% overhead. Tetragon proved in-kernel enforcement. Owning the kernel command line (lsm=) and config (kprobe override) removes the deployment barrier.
opportunities.evidence: AgentSight paper and repository; Tetragon enforcement docs; BPF LSM kernel docs.
opportunities.risk: TLS probes break on statically linked or pinned TLS libraries, and false positives may annoy users. Begin in audit-only mode.

opportunities.idea: Per-agent egress firewall with credential injection: transparent redirection by cgroup (no reliance on proxy environment variables), DNS fencing, and a system CA so the proxy can inspect TLS and substitute credentials for allowed hosts.
opportunities.why_now: Hostname-only proxies can be bypassed by domain fronting, and Docker Sandboxes already proved that sentinel-credential injection works in a microVM.
opportunities.evidence: Claude Code security limitations; Docker Sandboxes architecture; srt Windows DNS caveat.
opportunities.risk: Intercepting TLS creates a high-value target, and certificate pinning in some tools will break.

opportunities.idea: Ship one image as both a bootable OS and a VM guest: boot on x86 with NVIDIA and on Asahi, and run as a libkrun or Apple Containerization guest on macOS so the founder can develop on the M1 Pro without rebooting.
opportunities.why_now: libkrun supports HVF and virtio-gpu (Venus or native context). Apple Containerization ships minimal kernels from 6.14.9. Asahi now covers M1 to M3.
opportunities.evidence: libkrun README; Apple Containerization README; Asahi blog and feature table.
opportunities.risk: GPU performance inside the VM, and Asahi's GPU kernel driver living outside mainline, may weaken the local-model story on Apple hardware.

opportunities.idea: Memory governor for model memory on unified-memory machines: use pressure-stall information (PSI) to load, unload and offload KV caches across agents, giving model memory its own quota so a 16 GB machine can multiplex models and agents.
opportunities.why_now: kvcached and Aegaeon proved that elastic KV and model memory pays off, but only for CUDA and ROCm; unified-memory machines (Apple Silicon, AMD APUs) lack an equivalent.
opportunities.evidence: kvcached README (CUDA and ROCm only); Aegaeon token-level scaling; cgroup v2 PSI interfaces.
opportunities.risk: Achievable in userland, so it is a weak moat. Its value comes from being on by default in the OS rather than from kernel exclusivity.

recommendations: Do not write a kernel. Build an image-based distribution (bootc or mkosi with systemd v258 or later) whose differentiator is secure-by-default policy composition. Kernel floor: Linux 6.15 or later (Landlock audit) with CONFIG_BPF_LSM, lsm= including landlock and bpf, CONFIG_SCHED_CLASS_EXT, CONFIG_CHECKPOINT_RESTORE and CONFIG_BPF_KPROBE_OVERRIDE enabled.

Make the first public demo 'agent undo': a Btrfs root, a subvolume per task, automatic snapshots around each agent action, and one command to roll back. It is the most visible capability that userland tools cannot match system-wide, and it carries the least kernel risk.

Build the agent principal layer on top of sandbox-runtime or bubblewrap rather than replacing them. Wrap every agent, MCP server and hook in a systemd transient unit with Landlock, a seccomp profile and a cgroup-scoped egress policy, and publish the policy format so other tools can target it.
Begin enforcement in audit-only mode: ship AgentSight-style eBPF correlation first, then promote rules to BPF LSM deny decisions once false-positive rates are measured and published.

Do not invest in kernel-level GPU scheduling (gpu_ext, LithOS) or the dmem cgroup on the M1 Pro: none apply to Apple GPUs under Linux. Use userland serving (llama.cpp, MLX on a macOS host, Pie or kvcached on NVIDIA) and keep GPU policy in user space.

Develop primarily in a VM guest on the M1 Pro (libkrun or krunkit, or Apple Containerization) and treat Asahi bare-metal boot as a periodic integration target. Publish an x86_64 ISO for users with NVIDIA GPUs, where checkpointing (cuda-checkpoint) and kvcached work.
Treat semantic file systems (LSFS) and context paging (MemGPT) as ordinary services, not kernel features. They do not require owning the OS, and the evidence for kernel placement is weak.
Publish reproducible benchmarks from day one (snapshot latency, sandbox overhead, egress-bypass test results), so the project separates itself from 'AI OS' marketing with hard evidence.

Write the threat model before writing code: decide whether AgentOS protects the host from the agent, the user's data from exfiltration, or both. The egress and TLS-interception design depends on that decision.
contrarian_signals: The best-known 'agent operating system' (AIOS) is a Python userland framework that calls itself an abstraction layer over the host kernel. It shows that agent scheduling and context management do not need OS ownership. Its last tagged release is March 2025.
Anthropic achieved an 84% cut in permission prompts and OpenAI ships cross-platform sandboxes without owning any OS, so much of the safety benefit is already available as a userland download.

The industry is moving the isolation boundary into microVMs (Docker Sandboxes, Apple Containerization, agent-sandbox with gVisor or Kata, Sprites). The valuable product may be a guest image, not a bootable host OS.
Both sandbox-runtime and the Claude Code docs note that a sandbox sharing the host kernel can be escaped through a kernel vulnerability. Owning the OS does not remove that risk; VMs reduce it.

Every kernel-level GPU scheduling result found (gpu_ext, LithOS) is NVIDIA-specific and needs patched drivers, and dmem cgroup support began with Intel xe only. On the founder's M1 Pro, none of these mechanisms exist.

On the M1 Pro, Asahi's GPU kernel driver is outside mainline and the Neural Engine driver is out of tree. Linux may therefore run local models worse than macOS with MLX on the same hardware, which undermines a 'fast local models' pitch on this hardware.
Snapshots are not undo for the outside world: Btrfs snapshots are non-recursive and not backups, Sprites restores only files, and no filesystem rollback can reverse an email sent or an API call made.
Cloning checkpoints for agent branching duplicates randomness and secrets (Firecracker warning), and cuda-checkpoint does not support UVM. 'Fork a running agent' is harder than it sounds.

LithOS and gpu_ext headline numbers are measured against weak baselines (MPS, framework offloading). Gains against the best prior systems are much smaller (for example, 1.18x for LithOS in mixed inference and training).
open_questions: Clarifying question for the founder: is the primary target hardware Apple Silicon (Asahi) or x86 with NVIDIA? GPU scheduling, checkpointing and KV-cache primitives are available only on the latter.

Clarifying question for the founder: would a single image that boots on bare metal and also runs as a VM guest satisfy 'bootable OS'? A VM guest captures most of the security value with far less hardware friction.
Which threat model comes first: host integrity, data exfiltration, or protecting users from destructive actions? Each points to a different first feature (sandbox, egress firewall, or undo).

Unverified because the search budget ran out: details of Windows Agent Workspace beyond the MCP containment docs; Falco's agent-specific rules; seL4 or Capsicum applied to agents; MIG supported-GPU list; Llumnix v1 architecture; Kernel version numbers for Landlock ABIs 8 to 11 (unverified).
How well does LLM inference perform on Asahi's Vulkan (Honeykrisp) driver compared with MLX on macOS for the same M1 Pro? No 2025-2026 benchmark was found.
Can the BPF LSM and Landlock policies be generated automatically from an agent's declared tool manifest (for example, MCP tool schemas) without overwhelming users with prompts?
Will Windows ODR's agent-account model reach general availability and set the de facto design pattern that Linux users expect?

research:existing_ai_distros.dimension: Existing AI-focused Linux distributions and OS images: inventory, traction and gaps (as of 2026-10-16)
research:existing_ai_distros.executive_summary:
No product yet treats agents as first-class OS principals. The market splits into four groups, and none combines a bootable image, agent-level permissions and memory-aware local model scheduling.

(1) Vendor appliance stacks. These are NVIDIA DGX OS 7.5.0 for DGX Spark (Ubuntu base, kernel 6.17, CUDA 13.0.2), Red Hat Enterprise Linux AI 3.x (a bootc image, inference only, supporting only NVIDIA CUDA and AMD ROCm) and Lambda Stack. All are tied to one hardware vendor and target enterprises or GPU owners. NVIDIA joins its parts together through more than 100 playbooks (step-by-step setup guides) rather than one designed system. Its issue tracker shows playbooks failing on fresh machines and GB10 throughput dropping 25 to 40 percent over uptime.

(2) Platform vendors adding AI layers. These are Canonical inference snaps (beta, 19 models, 52 GitHub stars), SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16 with MCP (tech preview) and Fedora's AI/ML SIG (packaging stalled on ROCm and libstdc++ breakage). Red Hat retired InstructLab: the repository is archived, and its parts became separate SDKs.

(3) Opinionated desktops. Omarchy is the breakout. It has 44,921 stars, reports 1.28 million ISO downloads in year one, and has $23.65 million pledged to a foundation. It now calls itself an "agentic" distribution. However, its launcher starts every coding agent with its permission prompts switched off ("yolo", "--dangerously-skip-permissions", "bypassPermissions"). Bluefin and Bluefin GDX (CentOS bootc with NVIDIA drivers, uv and nvtop) and Pop!_OS COSMIC offer GPU-ready desktops but little that is specific to agents.

(4) Agent runtimes and sandboxes outside any distro. These are OpenClaw (392k stars, 722 GitHub security advisories in 2026, 14 critical), NVIDIA OpenShell and NemoClaw (alpha, Apache-2.0), AIOS (a Python runtime, not bootable), RamaLama and Pinokio (scripts "can run anything").

Hard evidence points to three unserved needs:
- **OS-enforced agent permissions:** agents get their own identity, file and network policy, a credential broker and human approval.
- **Model scheduling for unified memory:** DGX Spark's documentation admits that cudaMemGetInfo under-reports and nvidia-smi shows memory as unsupported.
- **Verified, reversible agent execution:** signed action logs tied to atomic rollback.

Native Apple Silicon is also open territory. Omarchy supports it only in a VM, while Fedora Asahi Remix (Fedora 44, Vulkan 1.4, OpenCL 3.0) supports the M1 Pro.

The disconfirming evidence is strong. Omarchy has already taken the "agentic distro" label. OpenShell now runs on macOS, which weakens the case that a bootable OS is required. Even well-funded corporate efforts have stopped: Intel ended Clear Linux, and Red Hat archived InstructLab. Method note: the shared web search budget ran out after 16 searches. I made up for this with more than 30 direct primary-source reads (official docs, READMEs, build scripts, GitHub API data).

pain_points.title: Agents run with full user privileges; 'agentic' distros disable safeguards
pain_points.description: The only mainstream distro with built-in agents (Omarchy 4) starts every supported coding agent with its permission prompts bypassed. No distro offers OS-level, per-agent controls over filesystem, network, credentials or approvals. Agent runtimes themselves have a very large vulnerability surface.
pain_points.segment: Developers and power users running coding agents and autonomous agents locally
pain_points.evidence: The omarchy-agent script maps agents to flags such as 'claude --permission-mode auto', 'agy --dangerously-skip-permissions', 'copilot --allow-all', 'crush --yolo', 'grok --permission-mode bypassPermissions' and 'hermes --yolo'. Its comment says these agents 'run unattended'. OpenClaw has 722 published GitHub security advisories (14 critical, 249 high) from January to September 2026.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Sandboxes (OpenShell, NemoClaw, microsandbox, E2B) are add-ons that need Docker or Podman. They are alpha or early-stage and not built into the boot image, init system or desktop. Distros optimise for convenience, and agent CLIs each define their own permission model.
pain_points.quantified_impact: 722 advisories in about 9 months for one agent runtime; Omarchy reports 1.28M ISO downloads exposed to permission-bypass defaults
pain_points.current_solutions: NVIDIA OpenShell or NemoClaw (alpha), devcontainers (recommended by Bluefin, but that docs section is empty), manual Podman or firejail, cloud sandboxes (E2B)

pain_points.title: Unified-memory accounting and model scheduling are not handled by the OS
pain_points.description: On unified-memory machines (DGX Spark GB10, Apple Silicon), standard tools misreport memory. No OS component admits, evicts or shares models across agents according to real memory pressure. Users drop caches by hand or estimate from /proc/meminfo.
pain_points.segment: Local inference users on unified-memory hardware (DGX Spark, Apple Silicon, AMD Strix Halo)
pain_points.evidence: The DGX Spark known issues say nvidia-smi shows 'Memory-Usage: Not Supported' and cudaMemGetInfo under-reports allocatable memory. The suggested workaround is to estimate from MemAvailable and SwapFree, or to flush caches with drop_caches. The July 2026 release notes list 'improved out-of-memory handling' as a new item.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Inference engines (llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama) each manage only their own process. Canonical inference snaps choose an engine for one model at install time, not at runtime across models. Distros treat model serving as an application, not a system resource.
pain_points.quantified_impact: Not quantified publicly; NVIDIA needed a dedicated OOM fix in July 2026 and a BIOS option reserving 2 or 4 GB for the display
pain_points.current_solutions: Manual model sizing, Ollama keep-alive settings, by-hand /proc/meminfo checks, drop_caches

pain_points.title: AI OS images are tied to one hardware vendor and integrated through documentation, not design
pain_points.description: Each vendor image serves one silicon family. Integration of tools is left to playbooks that break as upstream components change.
pain_points.segment: Prosumers and small teams with mixed or non-NVIDIA hardware
pain_points.evidence: RHEL AI 3.5 'supports NVIDIA CUDA and AMD ROCm AI accelerators only'. DGX OS targets GB10 and DGX only. The Bluefin GDX build adds only NVIDIA drivers, uv and nvtop. Open DGX Spark playbook issues (August to October 2026) include txt2kg failing on a fresh machine, a gpt-oss-20b download returning 'Entry not found', a wrong vLLM tool-call parser, GB10 throughput dropping 25 to 40 percent over uptime, and lost network reachability.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Vendors optimise for their own silicon and enterprise support contracts. Community distros lack the testing hardware. Playbooks are cheaper to write than an integrated, continuously tested system.
pain_points.quantified_impact: Over 100 playbook directories in NVIDIA's repo; reported 25 to 40 percent sustained throughput loss on GB10 until a full power-off
pain_points.current_solutions: Vendor playbooks, NGC containers, Ubuntu LTS as the de facto default because vendor guides target it first

pain_points.title: Fine-tuning has been removed from or split off AI OS images
pain_points.description: The leading enterprise AI OS dropped its built-in tuning workflow and became inference only. Fine-tuning now lives in standalone apps and SDKs with no OS-level resource or safety integration.
pain_points.segment: Developers who want to adapt models locally and safely
pain_points.evidence: InstructLab announced on 2025-09-02 that it would split into sdg_hub and training_hub. The repository is archived (last push 2026-03-30). The RHEL AI 3.0 notes describe an inference platform and say 'There is no direct upgrade path from Red Hat Enterprise Linux AI 1.5'. Meanwhile, standalone tuning tools have large followings: Unsloth has 78,097 stars and LlamaFactory 75,502.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Tuning needs a lot of hardware and support. Vendors moved it to Kubernetes and OpenShift AI. Distros do not package fast-changing training stacks.
pain_points.quantified_impact: InstructLab: 1,418 stars when archived, versus 78k for Unsloth, an app-level tool
pain_points.current_solutions: Unsloth, LlamaFactory, Axolotl, torchtune, MLX-LM on macOS

pain_points.title: AI toolchain packaging is fragile across distros
pain_points.description: PyTorch, ROCm and CUDA versions change faster than distro release cycles. This causes stalled updates, crashes on aarch64 and unclear support matrices.
pain_points.segment: All Linux AI users, especially AMD and aarch64
pain_points.evidence: Fedora AI/ML SIG, 2026-08-27: PyTorch 2.13 for F45 is stalled because a libstdc++ update made ROCm unbuildable, and ROCm 10 will not ship in F45. The January 2026 meeting reported PyTorch segfaults on aarch64. Lambda Stack's page names no supported Ubuntu release. DGX Spark CUDA is 'verified only at software release', so newer features come only through NGC containers.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Licensing rules keep CUDA out of community repos. ROCm has ABI churn. Volunteer packagers are scarce (the SIG asks for more contributors).
pain_points.quantified_impact: Fedora 43, 44 and 45 ship PyTorch 2.8.0, 2.9.1 and 2.12.0 respectively, so users face three different stacks
pain_points.current_solutions: Containers (NGC, RamaLama images), uv or pip virtual environments, Ubuntu LTS with vendor repos

pain_points.title: One-click AI installers execute arbitrary scripts without real isolation
pain_points.description: Popular launchers install AI apps by running shell commands from community scripts. They offer only directory-level separation.
pain_points.segment: Hobbyists and creators installing local AI apps
pain_points.evidence: Pinokio's README script policy says scripts 'can run anything' and that admins may modify featured scripts after publication. Issues include 'Virus found in the latest review of Pinokio' (2026-01-28) and 'Security: please enable private vulnerability reporting' (2026-09-10). Pinokio has 8,260 stars.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Isolation would break many GPU and Python app installs. Launchers favour compatibility, and the OS provides no capability boundary for installed AI apps.
pain_points.quantified_impact: Not quantified
pain_points.current_solutions: Manual review of scripts, running in VMs, Flatpak (incomplete GPU and CUDA support)

pain_points.title: Risk that corporate AI distros and tools will be abandoned
pain_points.description: Users are cautious about committing to AI-specific OS projects because well-funded efforts are often shut down or merged into other products.
pain_points.segment: Early adopters and enterprises evaluating AI distros
pain_points.evidence: Intel ended Clear Linux 'effective immediately' with no further security patches (reported 2025-07-18). InstructLab is archived. System76's Tensorman has 206 stars with little activity. blendOS is read-only (last push 2025-10-21). Ollama Rucksack (a bootable Ollama ISO) has 9 stars and no commits since 2025-06-02.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Business priorities change. Niche distros lack the maintainers to keep up with AI stack churn.
pain_points.quantified_impact: Not quantified
pain_points.current_solutions: Staying on Ubuntu, Fedora or Arch, with AI tools installed as apps or containers
