players.name: NVIDIA DGX OS 7 / DGX Spark software stack
players.offering: Ubuntu 24.04-based DGX OS 7.5.0 with NVIDIA kernel 6.17, CUDA 13, DGX Dashboard, NVIDIA Sync, a Docker container runtime and NGC. Over 100 playbooks cover vLLM, SGLang, TRT-LLM, Unsloth, NemoClaw and OpenShell. Air-gapped and cloud-init ISOs arrived in April 2026.
players.gap_or_weakness: Locked to GB10 and DGX hardware. Integration relies on playbooks that break. Unified-memory reporting is a known issue. User reports describe throughput loss and network drops. Agent safety is an optional playbook, not the default.
players.traction: Playbooks repo has 1,436 stars; unit sales not public

players.name: Red Hat Enterprise Linux AI 3.x / Red Hat AI
players.offering: A bootc image on RHEL 9 with Red Hat AI Inference Server (vLLM), the Model Optimization Toolkit, and Hugging Face, ModelCar and OCI model formats. Supports NVIDIA CUDA and AMD ROCm.
players.gap_or_weakness: Inference only since InstructLab was retired. No direct upgrade path from 1.5 to 3.0. Subscription-gated. No agent permission model. No Apple Silicon or Intel GPU support.
players.traction: Docs at version 3.5 (2026); InstructLab archived with 1,418 stars

players.name: Canonical inference snaps (Ubuntu)
players.offering: Snap per model, with engines chosen by a lscompute hardware probe that filters and ranks engine manifests. 19 models, including Gemma 4, Qwen 3.x and Nemotron 3. Local standard API.
players.gap_or_weakness: Beta. Picks an engine per model at install time only, with no runtime scheduling across models or agents. Low community traction. Confinement and API details are thin in the docs.
players.traction: 52 GitHub stars; launched 2025-10-23 with Intel and Ampere

players.name: SUSE AI / SLES 16
players.offering: SLES 16 (GA 2025-11-04) with MCP host and server in tech preview for Cockpit and CLI. MCP in Rancher Prime and Multi-Linux Manager. AI Factory with NVIDIA in preview, with GA expected later in 2026.
players.gap_or_weakness: Agents are used to manage infrastructure, not agents as workloads. Kubernetes-centric. Analysts say it trails Red Hat on ecosystem depth. I found no openSUSE AI image.

players.name: Fedora AI/ML SIG
players.offering: Packages for PyTorch, ROCm, llama.cpp, Ollama (ROCm and Vulkan backends) and whisper.cpp. Meets every two weeks.
players.gap_or_weakness: Packaging stalls (ROCm and libstdc++), PyTorch segfaults on aarch64, no CUDA, no AI image or agent features.

players.name: Omarchy (Omacom / DHH)
players.offering: ISO install. First-boot choice of default agent. An agent panel. Crash notifications that send the agent to analyse coredumps. Multi-account agent usage tracking (Claude, Codex, Grok, Kimi). Installers for Claude, ChatGPT, Hermes, OpenClaw and others.
players.gap_or_weakness: Agents launch with permissions bypassed and have no sandbox. No local model scheduling. x86 focus, with Apple Silicon only through a VM. A desktop aesthetic rather than a safety model.
players.traction: 44,921 stars; 1.28M ISO downloads in year one (self-reported); $23.65M pledged

players.name: Universal Blue Bluefin / Bluefin GDX / Aurora
players.offering: Bluefin ships Goose, Docker Model Runner, Podman AI Lab and Alpaca, plus Homebrew AI CLIs (claude-code, codex, gemini-cli). GDX is a CentOS Stream bootc image with NVIDIA open drivers, the container toolkit, uv and nvtop, built for x86_64 and aarch64.
players.gap_or_weakness: AI support is a set of tools added on top. The docs section on agent isolation is empty. GDX is NVIDIA-only and thin. There is no permission model.

players.name: Pop!_OS 24.04 with COSMIC (System76)
players.offering: Ubuntu 24.04 base, COSMIC Epoch 1 desktop written in Rust, preinstalled NVIDIA driver 580, ARM64 images.
players.gap_or_weakness: No AI or agent features. Tensorman (TensorFlow containers) has little activity. Reviewers report audio and screen-recording bugs.

players.name: Lambda Stack
players.offering: One-command install of drivers, CUDA 12.8, PyTorch 2.7, TensorFlow 2.19, JAX 0.6, NCCL and the container toolkit.
players.gap_or_weakness: NVIDIA and Ubuntu only. No stated Ubuntu version. Training-framework era, with nothing for agents or local LLM serving.

players.name: Pinokio
players.offering: JSON and shell scripts that install and run AI apps under ~/pinokio, with a Discover catalogue.
players.gap_or_weakness: Scripts 'can run anything'. Separation is only by directory. A virus report and a vulnerability-reporting request are open. Not an OS.

players.name: NVIDIA OpenShell / NemoClaw
players.category: Agent sandbox runtime and reference stack
players.offering: Policy-enforced sandboxes covering files, syscalls and network egress. Credential injection only for approved endpoints. Formal verification of policy changes. Container or microVM drivers. GPU passthrough through CDI.
players.gap_or_weakness: Alpha. Needs Docker or Podman. Not integrated with the OS. Isolation mechanisms are not specified in the docs. Telemetry on by default. The VM driver supports one GPU.

players.name: AIOS (agiresearch)
players.offering: A Python kernel abstraction for LLM, memory, storage and tool management, plus an agent SDK.
players.gap_or_weakness: Userspace only, not bootable. The Rust scheduler is a placeholder. Last listed release is March 2025.

players.name: RamaLama (containers project)
players.offering: Detects GPUs (CUDA, ROCm, Vulkan, Intel, Asahi). Runs rootless with read-only model mounts. 'ramalama run' has no network by default.
players.gap_or_weakness: Alpha. 'ramalama serve' publishes on 0.0.0.0. MLX bypasses containers. No scheduling across models.

players.name: openEuler Intelligence (EulerCopilot)
players.offering: RAG, workflow orchestration and an MCP preview on openEuler.
players.gap_or_weakness: Migrated to AtomGit. Integration into OS releases is undocumented on the page I read.

players.name: Fedora Asahi Remix
players.offering: Fedora 44 on M1 and M2 (M3 listed in device tables). Vulkan 1.4 and OpenCL 3.0 GPU drivers.
players.gap_or_weakness: No Neural Engine support. No AI integration. Hardware support lags newer chips.

players.name: Ollama Rucksack and similar single-purpose ISOs
players.offering: Debian Live ISO with Ollama, XFCE, optionally bundled models and network drivers blacklisted.
players.gap_or_weakness: Abandoned, with no commits since June 2025. No GPU documentation. A demo rather than an OS.

trends: Agents are moving into the distro layer, but for convenience rather than safety. Omarchy 4 adds first-boot agent selection, coredump-to-agent diagnosis and an agent panel. SLES 16 adds an MCP host and server. Bluefin ships Goose.

Image-based (bootc or ostree) operating systems are now the standard base for AI images. Examples are RHEL AI 3.x, Bluefin LTS and GDX on CentOS bootc, and Fedora Atomic derivatives. These give atomic updates and rollback that an agent 'undo' feature could build on.

Hardware-aware model packaging is spreading: Canonical lscompute-ranked engines, RamaLama GPU detection, and AMD Lemonade (5,912 stars). All of it works per model rather than as system-wide scheduling.

Agent sandboxing is forming as its own layer, outside any OS. Examples are NVIDIA OpenShell and NemoClaw (since February to March 2026), microsandbox (8,706 stars), Rivet agentOS (Wasm, 4,792 stars), E2B, gVisor and Firecracker.

Enterprise vendors are retreating to inference only and Kubernetes-scale serving (RHEL AI 3, llm-d with 4,837 stars, SUSE AI Factory). Fine-tuning has moved into separate SDKs (training_hub, sdg_hub) and apps such as Unsloth and LlamaFactory.
Vendors increasingly integrate through playbooks (NVIDIA's 100+), which creates ongoing breakage and opens room for continuously tested, declarative integration.

Agent runtimes have exploded in popularity and attack surface: OpenClaw has 392k stars and 722 advisories in 2026. This pushes demand for containment that does not rely on each agent's own permission prompts.

Corporate AI distro projects are consolidating or dying (Clear Linux ended in July 2025, InstructLab archived in March 2026). Community-led opinionated distros backed by large foundations are gaining momentum (Omarchy).

opportunities.idea: Agents as OS principals: an 'agentd' broker that gives each agent its own identity (uid or systemd slice), Landlock and seccomp filesystem and syscall policy, network-namespace egress allowlists, a credential proxy, and approval prompts handled by the OS rather than by each agent CLI.
opportunities.why_now: Agent CLIs are being run in 'yolo' mode by default on popular distros. OpenClaw's advisory volume shows that agent-level permissions cannot be trusted. OpenShell shows the policy model works but remains an alpha add-on.
opportunities.evidence: Omarchy omarchy-agent bypass flags; 722 OpenClaw advisories; OpenShell needs Docker or Podman and does not document its kernel mechanisms; Bluefin's devcontainer isolation docs section is empty.
opportunities.risk: NVIDIA could ship OpenShell by default in DGX OS, or Omarchy could add sandboxing quickly. Fine-grained policy may annoy users into switching it off, as happened with SELinux.

opportunities.idea: A memory-aware local model scheduler that runs as a system service. It admits, evicts and shares models across agents based on real unified-memory pressure, and exposes one OpenAI-compatible endpoint with per-agent quotas.
opportunities.why_now: DGX Spark documentation admits that memory reporting breaks on unified memory. Inference snaps and RamaLama choose engines but do not schedule. A 16 GB M1 Pro forces strict admission control.
opportunities.evidence: DGX Spark known issues (cudaMemGetInfo, nvidia-smi); the July 2026 OOM fix; inference-snaps engine auto-selection runs at install time only.
opportunities.risk: Ollama or llama.cpp could add a multi-model scheduler upstream, which would remove the OS-level advantage.

opportunities.idea: Verified, reversible agent execution: signed, hash-chained logs of agent actions tied to bootc, ostree or btrfs snapshots, giving a one-command 'undo what the agent did'.
opportunities.why_now: Image-based operating systems already provide atomic rollback. No product links rollback to agent sessions.
opportunities.evidence: The RHEL AI and Bluefin bootc bases have rollback. SLES 16 promotes 'Instant Rollback' for administrators, not for agents. No surveyed project offers agent action attestation.
opportunities.risk: Rollback covers system state only; it cannot undo external side effects such as sent emails or API calls. That limit must be stated honestly.

opportunities.idea: aarch64-first image that boots natively on Apple Silicon (through an Asahi base) and on GB10 or Arm servers, with the same agent and model layer on x86_64 with NVIDIA.
opportunities.why_now: Omarchy supports Apple Silicon only in a VM. Bluefin GDX already builds for aarch64 and the NVIDIA SBSA repository. Asahi supports the M1 Pro with Vulkan 1.4, and RamaLama supports the Asahi GPU.
opportunities.evidence: omarchy.org VM-only note; Bluefin LTS build-gdx aarch64 overrides; asahilinux.org/fedora conformance list.
opportunities.risk: No Neural Engine or CUDA on Asahi. Vulkan llama.cpp performance on an M1 Pro is far below macOS MLX. Asahi lags on M3 and newer chips.

opportunities.idea: Safe fine-tuning jobs as OS-managed workloads: small-model LoRA or QLoRA runs inside sandboxes with resource quotas, using recipes from Unsloth or LlamaFactory and dataset provenance.
opportunities.why_now: RHEL AI dropped InstructLab, which leaves no OS-integrated tuning path, while tuning apps have more than 75k stars each.
opportunities.evidence: InstructLab archive notice; Unsloth 78,097 stars; LlamaFactory 75,502 stars.
opportunities.risk: 16 GB of unified memory limits tuning to roughly 1B to 8B parameter models. Tuning stacks change quickly, which makes packaging expensive for a solo maintainer.

recommendations: Do not build a distro from scratch. Derive AgentOS from a bootc base, either Fedora Atomic or CentOS Stream using Universal Blue's build tooling (which Bluefin GDX already builds for aarch64 and x86_64). Keep the whole OS as one Containerfile so that one part-time maintainer can rebuild it in CI each night.

Pick one hero differentiator and make it the reason for the project: OS-enforced agent permissions (per-agent identity, Landlock and seccomp, network-namespace egress allowlist, credential proxy, desktop approval prompts). Ship it as a small Rust or Go daemon with declarative policy files, and make it able to wrap existing agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, Hermes) unchanged.

Evaluate NVIDIA OpenShell (Apache-2.0) as the enforcement backend before writing your own. Contribute an OS-native, non-Docker driver instead of competing. Verify its actual kernel mechanisms and turn off its default telemetry in your image.

Make 'agent undo' the second feature: snapshot the home directory and system subvolumes (btrfs or ostree) at the start of each agent session, and record signed, hash-chained action logs. Document plainly that external side effects cannot be rolled back.

Build the model layer as a thin scheduler over llama.cpp (Vulkan, CUDA, ROCm) and vLLM, served through one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Use MemAvailable and swap-based admission control with per-agent token and memory quotas. Reuse Canonical's lscompute-style hardware manifests rather than writing a new hardware probe.

Treat the M1 Pro as both your development machine and a first-class target: test images in a UTM or QEMU aarch64 VM every day, and boot natively through a Fedora Asahi Remix base for hardware tests. Set the default model size for 16 GB machines at about 4B to 8B parameters, quantised.

Replace playbooks with continuously tested, declarative 'capability packs' (for example, coding agent plus local model plus egress policy). Run them through CI smoke tests on every image build, because NVIDIA's playbook breakage shows what happens without this.

Do not compete with Omarchy on desktop polish or with Red Hat on enterprise inference. Position AgentOS as 'the safe place to let agents act': publish a threat model and a red-team test suite. Reproducible agent-escape tests become the main marketing material.

Limit fine-tuning to sandboxed LoRA jobs on small models, using existing tools (Unsloth or LlamaFactory recipes on Linux; note that MLX does not run on Linux). Defer anything larger until a contributor with suitable hardware joins.

Reduce abandonment risk from day one: Apache-2.0 licence, a minimal set of custom components, upstream contributions to OpenShell, RamaLama and llama.cpp, and a documented path for users to remove the AgentOS layer and keep a working Fedora system.
contrarian_signals: The 'agentic distro' label is already taken. Omarchy calls itself agentic, reports 1.28M ISO downloads in year one, has 44.9k stars and has $23.65M pledged. Being a novel AI-native distro is not a differentiator.

Agent safety is becoming portable and OS-independent. OpenShell supports Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon and WSL2, and NemoClaw is tested on Ubuntu, macOS and WSL. A bootable OS may not be needed to solve the main safety problem.

Practitioner guidance says distro choice matters less than GPU, VRAM and drivers, and recommends plain Ubuntu (OpenSourceFeed, 2026-07-09). Most users get local AI through cross-platform apps (Ollama 183k stars, LM Studio).
Canonical's inference snaps, backed by a major vendor, have only 52 GitHub stars a year after launch. This suggests weak demand for packaging models at the OS level.

Well-funded corporate efforts in this area have been shut down or broken up (Intel Clear Linux ended in 2025, InstructLab archived in 2026). This is a warning about sustainability for a solo, part-time project.
Enterprise leaders moved away from local fine-tuning in the OS towards inference only and Kubernetes serving. This suggests tuning on a 16 GB device is a niche feature.

Asahi Linux on an M1 Pro has no Neural Engine support and no MLX. Local inference performance on a natively booted AgentOS will be well below macOS on the same machine, which weakens the 'fast' promise on the founder's own hardware.

One third-party RHEL AI 3.4 guide (lucaberton.com) still lists InstructLab as a core component, which contradicts Red Hat's docs and the archived repository. Secondary coverage in this space is often unreliable.
open_questions: Clarifying question for the founder: who is the primary user? Is it a developer running coding agents on a laptop, a home-lab owner with an NVIDIA GPU or DGX Spark, or an organisation that needs auditable agents? Each points to a different base image and threat model.

Clarifying question for the founder: what does 'revolutionary' mean in measurable terms? Is it agent safety (escape-test pass rate), speed (tokens per second, time to first agent) or zero-configuration setup? The current brief asks for 'safely and fast' without ranking the two, and they conflict on 16 GB hardware.

Clarifying question for the founder: must the first release boot natively on Apple Silicon, or is a VM on the M1 Pro plus native x86_64 with NVIDIA acceptable? Native Asahi support adds kernel and GPU risk.

Method limitation: the shared web search budget ran out after 16 of the required 20 searches. I made up for this with more than 30 direct primary-source reads, but some areas remain unverified: openSUSE AI images, Ubuntu 26.04 AI features, Warmwind and other closed 'AI OS' products, and Chinese AI distros (openKylin, deepin UOS AI).
Which kernel mechanisms does OpenShell actually use (Landlock, seccomp, netns), and is a driver without Docker feasible? The public docs I read do not say.
What are the real adoption numbers for DGX OS (Spark unit sales), Pop!_OS installs and inference snap installs? None is published.
What is the release date of RHEL AI 3.0, and does Red Hat's Training Hub return to RHEL AI in a later 3.x release? Official release notes pages are thin.
Can Vulkan llama.cpp on Asahi with 16 GB deliver usable speed for 7B to 8B models compared with MLX on macOS? Independent benchmarks are needed before committing to native Apple Silicon support.
Will Omarchy add sandboxing in response to criticism of its permission-bypass defaults? Monitor its issue tracker and AGENTS.md.

research:bootable_tooling.dimension: Image-based Linux build tooling for a bootable AI OS maintained by one person
research:bootable_tooling.executive_summary:
Recommendation: build AgentOS as a bootc (bootable OCI) image based on CentOS Stream 10, set up the way Universal Blue builds its images: a Containerfile, GitHub Actions, cosign signing, and prebuilt signed NVIDIA open kernel modules. Ship heavy AI stacks as pinned OCI containers. Do not bake them into /usr. This is the only base that meets all four needs together. A tiny team already ships at scale on it. NVIDIA and CUDA already work on an immutable system with Secure Boot. x86_64 and aarch64 images can both be built for free in CI. The required skill is writing Containerfiles, not learning a new language.

Evidence: Bazzite, built the Universal Blue way, passed 100,000 weekly active devices (15 Oct 2026). Bluefin GDX already ships CentOS Stream 10 with NVIDIA drivers, CUDA, RamaLama and uv, on x86_64 and aarch64, with Secure Boot (Sep 2025). bootc release 1.17.0 (6 Oct) declared its composefs backend stable, and its CLI and API are stable. It is still only a CNCF Sandbox project. GitHub gives public repositories free x64 and arm64 runners (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 14 GB SSD). AMD lists RHEL 10.x as supported for ROCm, but not Fedora or NixOS, which favours a RHEL-family base.

NixOS is the strongest rival on reproducibility but the weakest fit for a solo AI OS. The default cache.nixos.org does not hold CUDA builds. The community CUDA cache moved and has no coverage for stable releases (Dec 2025). Flox only caches builds from its own fork that follows the unstable branch. nixified-ai deprecated most of its packages for lack of funding. lanzaboote, which gives NixOS Secure Boot, is not yet part of nixpkgs.

Other options are a poor fit:
- Ubuntu Core ties the project to the Snap Store.
- Talos and Flatcar are Kubernetes and server appliances.
- mkosi and ParticleOS follow the ideal verified-boot design, but ParticleOS says it is unstable, and its prebuilt images are x86-64 only.

Heavy stacks: vLLM ships binaries compiled for CUDA 12.9 that do not work with other CUDA or PyTorch builds. Baking it into the base OS therefore guarantees conflicts. Use one OCI image per accelerator, as RamaLama does. Optionally use bootc logically bound images for one default runtime. Keep sysexts for small host tools only.

Critical constraint: the M1 Pro cannot test NVIDIA, x86 Secure Boot or TPM measured boot. Cross-architecture builds under emulation run 8 to 10 times slower. Build in CI, and buy one x86_64 test machine with an NVIDIA GPU. Sealed UKI and composefs images were test-only in April 2026, so postpone measured boot.

Method note: the shared web-search budget ran out after 6 searches. These findings rest on about 40 direct reads of primary sources.

pain_points.title: NVIDIA kernel modules and Secure Boot on immutable images
pain_points.description: Immutable images cannot compile NVIDIA modules on the host at runtime. The modules have to be built and signed at image build time, matched exactly to the image kernel, and their signing key has to be enrolled as a MOK on every machine. When the kernel and driver versions drift apart, systems fail to boot or lose GPU acceleration.
pain_points.segment: Maintainers of image-based Linux distributions aimed at GPU and AI users
pain_points.evidence: Universal Blue runs a separate akmods pipeline that publishes prebuilt modules daily, grouped as nvidia, nvidia-open and zfs, for six kernel flavours. It sometimes pins the CoreOS kernel when ZFS modules cannot build against it. On Flatcar, building the driver from source takes 5-10 minutes at first boot and cannot work with Secure Boot; only the prebuilt signed sysext can. Fedora users report that a new kernel blocked NVIDIA loading (Jun 2025) and that driver 610 broke package dependencies (May 2026). Talos says its NVIDIA drivers are tied to a specific Talos release.
pain_points.quantified_impact: First-boot compile adds 5-10 minutes and makes Secure Boot impossible (Flatcar docs). Every kernel bump needs matching rebuilt modules.
pain_points.current_solutions: ublue-os/akmods prebuilt signed modules copied in with COPY --from; Flatcar prebuilt sysext signed with a key thrown away after the build; Talos nonfree-kmod-nvidia extensions; negativo17 akmod, DKMS and RHEL kABI modules; NVIDIA open modules by default from R560.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: NVIDIA kernel modules are out-of-tree. The proprietary flavour cannot ship in-tree, and nova_core is not production-ready. Every distribution has to run its own signing and key-enrolment process.

sources.title: negativo17 NVIDIA driver page and comments

pain_points.title: Dependency conflicts in heavy AI stacks (CUDA, PyTorch, vLLM, SGLang)
pain_points.description: Each inference engine pins its own versions of CUDA, PyTorch and Python. Installing two engines into one system /usr, or onto the host's Python, breaks one of them. On an image-based OS a host-level conflict also blocks the whole image build.
pain_points.segment: Users and builders of local LLM serving and fine-tuning
pain_points.evidence: The vLLM docs say its precompiled binaries target CUDA 12.9 (with 12.8 and 13.0 builds) and are incompatible with other CUDA or PyTorch builds. They recommend uv with a fresh environment and warn against conda-installed PyTorch. The ROCm wheels require Python 3.12.
pain_points.quantified_impact: Each engine needs its own environment. Reusing an existing PyTorch install requires building vLLM from source (vLLM docs).
pain_points.current_solutions: Per-engine OCI images (vllm/vllm-openai; RamaLama images for CUDA, ROCm, Vulkan and Intel), uv virtual environments, Nix closures and Flox environments.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Upstream projects compile against specific CUDA and PyTorch ABIs and release fast. No distribution can keep one shared set of versions coherent.

pain_points.title: Developing on Apple Silicon cannot validate the target hardware
pain_points.description: An M1 Pro can build and boot aarch64 Linux in a VM. It cannot test NVIDIA or CUDA, x86 UEFI Secure Boot, or TPM 2.0 measured boot, and x86_64 builds run under slow emulation. The main bootc test tools assume a Linux host with libvirt or QEMU.
pain_points.segment: Solo founders and indie maintainers who use Macs
pain_points.evidence: The image-builder README marks cross-architecture builds as experimental and 8-10 times slower than native builds. The bcvk article requires a RHEL 10 host with Podman and libvirt. podman-bootc was archived on 3 Jun 2026 in favour of bcvk. Fedora Asahi Remix 44 supports the M1 Pro, but Asahi has no NVIDIA support.
pain_points.quantified_impact: Emulated cross-architecture builds run 8-10x slower. GPU and Secure Boot paths cannot be tested on the Mac at all.
pain_points.current_solutions: podman machine (applehv) for aarch64 builds; free GitHub arm64 and x64 runners; a separate x86 test machine or a rented cloud GPU.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Apple Silicon does not offer standard UEFI Secure Boot or TPM for Linux, and it cannot host NVIDIA GPUs. The tooling vendors target Linux workstations.

sources.title: Test and deploy bootable containers with bcvk

pain_points.title: CUDA binary caching and licensing on NixOS
pain_points.description: CUDA is unfree, so cache.nixos.org does not hold CUDA builds. Users must trust third-party caches whose coverage depends on which nixpkgs revision they pin. A cache miss means compiling PyTorch or CUDA packages locally for hours.
pain_points.segment: NixOS ML users and anyone considering NixOS as an AI OS base
pain_points.evidence: The NixOS wiki says the Foundation does not cache CUDA packages and that large builds can freeze weaker machines. On Discourse (Dec 2025), maintainers said the cache moved to cache.nixos-cuda.org and that stable branches are not cached. Flox builds from its own fork that follows the unstable branch, so pinned channel revisions are unlikely to get cache hits. nixified-ai deprecated its InvokeAI and textgen packages for lack of funding.
pain_points.quantified_impact: No cache for stable releases (Dec 2025), so systems pinned to stable rebuild CUDA software locally.
pain_points.current_solutions: cache.nixos-cuda.org; the Flox CUDA catalog, which has an NVIDIA redistribution agreement; following nixos-unstable.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Funding depends on volunteer maintainers, and NVIDIA's licence limits redistribution to approved parties.

pain_points.title: Churn in image-build tooling
pain_points.description: Tools for building and testing bootable images keep being renamed, moved or archived. Composefs and sealed images are moving from experimental to stable at different speeds in different projects, so documentation contradicts itself.
pain_points.segment: Small teams building on bootc, OSTree or Nix image tooling
pain_points.evidence: podman-bootc archived on 3 Jun 2026. bootc-image-builder source moved into osbuild/image-builder. nixos-generators archived on 30 Jan 2026. The OSTree composefs docs say 'do not deploy to production systems yet', while bootc 1.17.0 calls its composefs backend stable.
pain_points.quantified_impact: Three major tools archived or relocated within 12 months.
pain_points.current_solutions: Pin tool versions, follow the Universal Blue templates, and let Renovate update digests.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: The ecosystem is converging fast, and maintainers are consolidating tools.

pain_points.title: ROCm support outside Ubuntu and the RHEL family
pain_points.description: AMD officially supports ROCm only on a short list of enterprise distributions. Fedora, NixOS and immutable distributions are not on it, so an AMD-first AI OS takes on support risk.
pain_points.segment: AMD GPU owners running local AI
pain_points.evidence: The ROCm system requirements page (2026-07-15) lists Ubuntu 24.04 and 22.04, RHEL 10.1, 10.0 and 9.x, SLES 15 SP7, Debian 13 and 12, Rocky 9 and Oracle Linux. It does not list Fedora or NixOS. The NixOS wiki says ROCm packages are cached on Hydra but that local compiles can still happen. The vLLM ROCm wheels cover only ROCm 7.0 and 7.2.1.
pain_points.quantified_impact: Fedora and NixOS are absent from the official support matrix.
pain_points.current_solutions: ROCm containers on the host's in-tree amdgpu driver; Fedora community packaging; nixpkgs rocmSupport.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: AMD focuses its validation on enterprise and LTS distributions.

pain_points.title: CI disk and time limits for multi-gigabyte AI images
pain_points.description: Free CI runners have little disk space for building and rechunking images that contain the CUDA userspace, and for generating ISOs.
pain_points.segment: Open-source distribution maintainers who rely on free CI
pain_points.evidence: Standard GitHub-hosted Linux runners for public repositories, x64 and arm64, have 4 CPUs, 16 GB RAM and a 14 GB SSD.
pain_points.quantified_impact: 14 GB SSD per job.
pain_points.current_solutions: Steps that free disk space, rechunking, splitting the image build from the disk-image build (the image-template has build.yml and build-disk.yml), and external storage through rclone to S3.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Free-tier economics.

pain_points.title: Measured boot and sealed images clash with customisation
pain_points.description: A boot chain verified with UKI, composefs and TPM limits changes to the kernel command line and the use of third-party kernel modules. The tooling is not yet production-ready.
pain_points.segment: Security-focused image OS builders
pain_points.evidence: Fedora's sealed Atomic Desktop images (28 Apr 2026) require Secure Boot, are not signed with Fedora keys, and carry the warning not to use them in production. Kairos Trusted Boot says a change to the kernel command line needs a rebuilt image. The 2022 systemd design described signed PCR policies as future work at that time.
pain_points.quantified_impact: No production-ready sealed Fedora or bootc image exists as of April 2026.
pain_points.current_solutions: Kairos Trusted Boot, ParticleOS, Ubuntu Core FDE, lanzaboote on NixOS.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Supporting signed third-party modules, managing keys and recovering from mistakes are still hard problems.

players.name: bootc and Fedora/CentOS bootc base images (Red Hat, Fedora, CentOS)
players.offering: Transactional OS updates and rollback delivered as OCI images. Stable CLI and API, ostree default backend, composefs backend stable in 1.17.0. Logically bound images tie app containers to OS updates. Install via to-disk using systemd-repart.
players.gap_or_weakness: CNCF Sandbox. Sealed images are test-only. Tooling churn (podman-bootc archived, BIB moved). Test tools assume a Linux host. Bound images do not support rootless containers or Anaconda.
players.traction: 1,275 contributors per CNCF; RHEL image mode; Rocky bootc via CIQ (Feb 2026)

players.name: Universal Blue (Bluefin, Aurora, Bazzite, akmods, image-template)
players.offering: Containerfile plus GitHub Actions plus Renovate plus cosign. Prebuilt signed NVIDIA open and proprietary and ZFS modules published as OCI images. Template for custom images with ISO and qcow2 generation.
players.gap_or_weakness: Scope cuts in 2025. Secure Boot needs MOK enrollment. Kernel pins when ZFS or NVIDIA lag. Mostly desktop-focused.
players.traction: Bazzite >100k weekly devices (Oct 2026); Bluefin repo 3,111 commits, 2.6k stars

players.name: Bluefin GDX / Bluefin LTS
players.offering: CentOS Stream 10 plus NVIDIA drivers plus CUDA plus RamaLama plus uv, x86_64 and aarch64, Secure Boot
players.gap_or_weakness: NVIDIA only. No agent orchestration layer. No local layering. HWE branch lacks Secure Boot.

players.name: NixOS plus Nixpkgs CUDA team
players.offering: Whole-system closures, generation rollback, build-image for ISO and raw, cudaSupport and rocmSupport flags
players.gap_or_weakness: No CUDA on cache.nixos.org; no cache for stable releases; Secure Boot via lanzaboote not yet in nixpkgs; steep learning curve; ML flakes underfunded

players.category: Nix-based environment manager with CUDA redistribution
players.offering: NVIDIA-approved prebuilt CUDA, PyTorch and ONNX closures in a public cache
players.gap_or_weakness: Builds only from its own fork that follows unstable; depends on volunteer nixpkgs maintainers

players.offering: Immutable system with automatic rollback, FDE, Ubuntu Core 26, CUDA workloads and Jetson guides

trends: Bootable OCI images are becoming the shared delivery format across vendors: bootc entered the CNCF in Jan 2025, CIQ shipped Rocky bootc images in Feb 2026, Fedora built sealed test images in Apr 2026, and bootc declared composefs stable in Oct 2026.
Verified boot chains (signed UKI, composefs or dm-verity, TPM-bound disk unlock) are moving from design documents (systemd 2022) to test images (Fedora 2026). Production readiness is still pending.

NVIDIA's open kernel modules became the default (R560, 2024), and CUDA is now redistributed by OS vendors and Flox (2025). Packaging is getting simpler, but module signing is still each distribution's job.
systemd-sysext is spreading as the way to deliver optional host components: Flatcar sysext-bakery, fedora-sysexts, and Talos system extensions.
Free native arm64 CI (GA Aug 2025) removes the need for cross-architecture emulation for open-source projects.
Image tooling is consolidating: podman-bootc into bcvk, bootc-image-builder into image-builder, nixos-generators into nixpkgs.
AI workstation images already exist (Bluefin GDX). Whether the OS layer can be a differentiator is shrinking.
Small teams are shrinking their scope to survive, for example the 2025 cuts to ublue-os/main.

opportunities.idea: Containers by default for AI runtimes: the OS detects the GPU at first boot and pulls a matching, signed runtime image (CUDA, ROCm, Vulkan or CPU), pinned by digest and tied to the OS release through bootc logically bound images
opportunities.why_now: bootc logically bound images exist, RamaLama shows the one-image-per-accelerator pattern, and vLLM's CUDA pinning makes host-level installs unworkable
opportunities.evidence: bootc LBI docs; vLLM docs warn its binaries are incompatible with other CUDA or PyTorch builds; RamaLama ships CUDA, ROCm, Vulkan and Intel images
opportunities.risk: Bound images do not support rootless containers. Multi-gigabyte images make updates slow. RamaLama is alpha.

opportunities.idea: Attested agent host: use sealed UKI and composefs plus TPM measured boot so agents and remote model endpoints can verify that the host has not been modified
opportunities.why_now: Fedora's sealed images and bootc's stable composefs arrived in 2026. Agent security is a fresh concern.
opportunities.evidence: Fedora sealed test images (Apr 2026); bootc 1.17.0; ParticleOS and Kairos Trusted Boot designs
opportunities.risk: Not production-ready. Third-party NVIDIA modules complicate a sealed chain. It would take most of a solo maintainer's time.

opportunities.idea: Optional AI capability packs delivered as sysexts with systemd-sysupdate (for example inference CLIs, GPU monitoring and debugging tools), following the Flatcar bakery pattern
opportunities.why_now: systemd has mature sysext and sysupdate support (mutable mode since v256), and Flatcar already proves distribution through GitHub releases
opportunities.evidence: Flatcar sysext-bakery includes ollama and nvidia-runtime; fedora-sysexts publishes via sysupdate redirectors
opportunities.risk: No dependency resolution. Each pack must be rebuilt for every OS VERSION_ID or SYSEXT_LEVEL. Sysexts cannot easily carry kernel modules.

opportunities.idea: A Mac-first workflow for building an OS: local aarch64 builds and VM boots in podman machine, with CI handling x86_64, ISOs and GPU smoke tests
opportunities.why_now: Free arm64 runners and the aarch64 bootc base images make Apple Silicon a workable authoring platform. Few projects document this.
opportunities.evidence: GitHub arm64 GA (Aug 2025); Bluefin LTS and GDX aarch64 images; image-builder cross-architecture is 8-10x slower, so builds should be native per architecture
opportunities.risk: GPU and TPM paths still need real x86 hardware.

recommendations: Base: use a bootc image derived from quay.io/centos-bootc/centos-bootc:stream10, modelled on Bluefin LTS and GDX. This matches the RHEL 10 support listed by NVIDIA and ROCm and provides a kernel that stays put for the release lifetime. Add a Fedora-based edge variant only if users need GPUs that the 6.12 kernel cannot drive.

Start from ublue-os/image-template: Containerfile, build.yml, build-disk.yml, cosign key in SIGNING_SECRET, Renovate digest pinning. Publish to GHCR from a public repository so the free x64 and arm64 runners apply.

Ship only NVIDIA open kernel modules (Turing and newer) as prebuilt signed packages copied in at build time from ublue-os/akmods, or from your own akmods job using your own MOK key. Document the one-time MOK enrollment step. Formally drop support for Maxwell, Pascal and Volta.

Keep exactly two images and two architectures at launch: agentos (generic, Mesa/ROCm-ready) and agentos-nvidia, each built for x86_64 and aarch64. Universal Blue's 2025 scope cuts show the cost of each extra variant.

Never install vLLM, SGLang, PyTorch or CUDA userspace into /usr. Ship them as digest-pinned OCI images run with Podman and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit (CDI). Bind at most one default runtime with bootc logically bound images, and keep model weights in /var.
Use sysexts only for small optional host tools, with SYSEXT_LEVEL set and SHA256SUMS published for systemd-sysupdate, following the Flatcar sysext-bakery pattern.

Build every architecture natively in CI. Avoid emulated cross-architecture builds on the M1 Pro, which run 8-10x slower. Use podman machine on the Mac only for quick aarch64 builds and qcow2 boot checks in a VM.
Buy or rent one x86_64 test machine with a Turing-or-newer NVIDIA GPU and TPM 2.0, and run an install, upgrade and rollback test on it before every release.
Postpone sealed UKI and TPM measured boot until Fedora and bootc sealed images leave test status. In the meantime, choose a systemd-boot-compatible ESP layout so you can switch later.
Use Nix or Flox only inside containers or developer shells for reproducible agent toolchains. Do not use NixOS as the OS base unless the founder already writes Nix fluently.
contrarian_signals: bootc is still a CNCF Sandbox project. CNCF defines Sandbox as not yet widely tested in production.

Containerfile builds are not bit-for-bit reproducible, because dnf installs pull whatever packages are current at build time. NixOS gives stronger reproducibility, which undercuts the reproducibility argument for bootc.
The OSTree composefs docs still say not to deploy to production, while bootc 1.17.0 calls composefs stable. Readiness signals conflict.
Bluefin GDX already ships the base layer of an AI workstation: NVIDIA drivers, CUDA and RamaLama. A new OS base adds little that is new, so differentiation has to come from the agent layer.
Universal Blue cut image variants in 2025. If an established tiny team has to trim, a solo part-time maintainer should expect even less capacity.
NVIDIA breakages on Fedora (a kernel change blocking the driver in Jun 2025, driver 610 dependency failures in May 2026) show that fast-moving bases break proprietary GPU stacks.
Bazzite's 100k figure counts devices through DNF countme, not users, and the project reports it itself.
The M1 Pro cannot test NVIDIA, x86 Secure Boot or TPM. A Mac-only workflow cannot validate the product's core value.
Wanting a revolutionary bootable OS conflicts with working solo and part-time. Image-based bases are deliberately conventional, so the innovation budget belongs above the OS layer.
vLLM's own docs present Docker only as an option. Users may prefer pip or uv on a general-purpose distribution, which weakens the case for a bootable OS.
open_questions: Clarifying question: is AgentOS a desktop workstation, a headless agent appliance, or both? The answer decides between deriving from Bluefin LTS and starting from a minimal centos-bootc image.
Clarifying question: which accelerators must be first-class at launch: NVIDIA only, AMD ROCm, or Apple Silicon through Asahi? Each one multiplies the test matrix.
Not verified: does ublue-os/akmods publish modules for CentOS Stream 10 kernels, or does Bluefin LTS/GDX get its EL NVIDIA modules from elsewhere?
Will Fedora and bootc sealed images support third-party signed kernel modules such as NVIDIA's?
Do standard GitHub-hosted runners expose KVM for bcvk boot and rollback tests? Not verified.
What exactly are the redistribution terms for bundling NVIDIA CUDA userspace in an open-source OS image?

research:m1_dev_feasibility.dimension: Developing and testing a bootable AI OS on an Apple M1 Pro with 16 GB
research:m1_dev_feasibility.executive_summary:
Bottom line: the M1 Pro is a good machine for daily AgentOS development, but it should not be the main bare-metal target. It also cannot validate x86_64 plus NVIDIA builds. The best plan uses three tiers: macOS with VMs, Asahi dual-boot and cheap cloud or CI.

A note on method: the shared WebSearch budget ran out after 3 searches. The findings below rest on about 45 direct reads of primary sources, so some 2026 prices remain unverified.

- **Asahi status.** Fedora Asahi Remix 43 shipped on 18 March 2026, and version 44 was targeted for 28 April 2026. M1 Pro covers GPU, suspend, camera, speakers and battery in linux-asahi. Thunderbolt and DP Alt Mode are still WIP. Video encode is TBA, and the Neural Engine driver is out of tree.
- **GPU stack.** The stack is conformant for OpenGL 4.6, Vulkan 1.4 and OpenCL 3.0. However, the 21,000-line kernel GPU driver is still downstream (February 2026). The lead GPU developer left in August 2025, which is a bus-factor risk.
- **Inference on Asahi.** On a base M1, llama.cpp Vulkan reaches 38 t/s prompt processing (pp512) and 12.5 t/s generation (tg128). Metal on macOS reaches 118 and 14.2. Prompt processing on Linux is therefore about three times slower.
- **MLX on Linux.** It runs only on CPU or CUDA, so Asahi gets no MLX GPU path.
- **Inference in a macOS VM.** krunkit/libkrun exposes Vulkan compute (no rendering) through Venus and MoltenVK. Red Hat measured 74–80% of native Metal. A VM on macOS can therefore beat bare-metal Asahi for LLM work.
- **Other VM options.** Lima 2.0 includes an experimental krunkit driver. Apple's container tool (1.5.0, September 2026) needs macOS 26 and has no GPU support. UTM offers only VirGL OpenGL.
- **No nested virtualization.** It requires M3 or later, so KVM-based agent sandboxes can be tested only on bare-metal Asahi or x86 cloud.
- **16 GB memory.** macOS gives the GPU about 66.7% of RAM by default, roughly 10.7 GB. Dense 7–8B Q4 models run well (about 36 t/s on 7B Q4_0, M1 Pro 16-core). 14B is borderline, and 30B MoE models do not fit. QLoRA fine-tuning is realistic only at 8B or below.
- **Testing x86_64 and NVIDIA.** Public GitHub repositories get free x64 runners with KVM for QEMU boot tests, plus free arm64 runners. GitHub GPU runners (T4, $0.052/min) need a paid plan and cannot boot a custom OS. AWS g4dn.xlarge can boot custom AMIs for $0.33/hr spot or $0.53/hr on demand. RunPod RTX 3090/4090 pods ($0.22–0.34/hr) can test userspace only.

Estimated cost: $0 for tooling and about $15–40 per month for cloud.

pain_points.title: No first-class GPU ML stack for Linux on Apple Silicon
pain_points.description: On Asahi, the only GPU path is Mesa Vulkan (Honeykrisp) and OpenCL. Prompt processing in llama.cpp runs about three times slower than Metal on macOS. MLX has no Linux GPU backend for Apple hardware, and the Neural Engine is out of tree.
pain_points.segment: Solo developer building an AI OS on M1/M2 hardware
pain_points.evidence: Apple M1 on Asahi (Vulkan): pp512 38.29, tg128 12.47 t/s on Llama 2 7B Q4_0, against 117.96/14.15 on macOS Metal for the 8-core M1. A commenter attributes the gap to Honeykrisp. MLX documents only CPU (mlx[cpu]) and CUDA installs for Linux.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Apple publishes no GPU documentation, so the Linux stack depends on reverse engineering. The GPU lead left in August 2025, and team effort has moved to M3 bring-up and upstreaming.

sources.title: Dissecting the Apple M1 GPU, the end

pain_points.current_solutions: Use macOS Metal or MLX for inference and treat Asahi Vulkan as a functional test path only.
pain_points.quantified_impact: Prompt processing about 3x slower and token generation about 12% slower than macOS Metal on a base M1.

pain_points.title: Bare-metal Apple Silicon support depends on a downstream kernel
pain_points.description: A bootable AgentOS image for Apple Silicon needs the Asahi kernel fork, m1n1, Asahi U-Boot, firmware extracted by the Asahi installer, and a 16K-page kernel. It cannot be booted from USB on a fresh machine without first running the installer from macOS.
pain_points.segment: Distro builders targeting Apple Silicon
pain_points.evidence: The Asahi distro policy requires the Asahi kernel fork, m1n1, U-Boot and asahi-firmware. The GPU driver is about 21,000 lines and only began upstreaming in February 2026. The 7.2 report (August 2026) says GPU and DCP work remains too large to upstream. The NixOS Apple Silicon guide shows that USB boot via U-Boot works after a 'UEFI environment only' install.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Upstreaming is slow, the project lost its founder (February 2025) and GPU lead (August 2025), and Apple's boot chain requires the installer step from macOS.
pain_points.current_solutions: Build on top of Fedora Asahi Remix packages, or follow the nixos-apple-silicon model.
pain_points.quantified_impact: More than 1,000 downstream patches were cited in February 2025, with a 95,000 to 83,000 line reduction reported in February 2026.

pain_points.title: GPU access in macOS VMs is limited
pain_points.description: Apple's Virtualization.framework gives Linux guests no 3D acceleration. krunkit/libkrun exposes Vulkan compute only (no rendering) through Venus and MoltenVK, and Lima's krunkit driver is experimental. UTM offers only experimental VirGL OpenGL.
pain_points.segment: Developers testing GPU-dependent Linux images on Macs
pain_points.evidence: Podman Desktop says macOS GPU support covers only Vulkan compute shaders, not rendering or draw. Red Hat measured 74–80% of native Metal (20.84 t/s for llama3.1:8b on an M4 Pro). Lima's krunkit driver needs Lima 2.0 or later and macOS 14 or later, and is experimental. A 2024 design note set an 8 GB GPU memory cap.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Apple offers no paravirtual GPU for Linux guests, and translation layers add overhead. KosmicKrisp (Vulkan on Metal 4) needs macOS 26.

sources.title: How we improved AI inference on macOS Podman containers
Enabling containers to access the GPU on macOS

pain_points.current_solutions: krunkit through Podman machine (libkrun provider), Lima, or RamaLama. Alternatively, run inference on the host and expose it to the guest over an API.
pain_points.quantified_impact: 20–26% throughput loss against native Metal, with no graphics rendering.

pain_points.title: No nested virtualization on M1
pain_points.description: KVM is unavailable inside Linux VMs on the M1 Pro. Firecracker, Kata and microVM-per-agent sandboxes therefore cannot be tested in a VM on the development Mac.
pain_points.segment: AI OS builders using microVM agent sandboxes
pain_points.evidence: Lima's template states that nested virtualization is supported with vz or krunkit only on Apple M3 or later with macOS 15 or later. GitHub macOS runners also lack nested virtualization.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Hardware support for nested virtualization arrived only with M3.
pain_points.current_solutions: Run sandboxes on bare-metal Asahi, which has KVM and DRM native context, or on x86 KVM in GitHub Actions.
pain_points.quantified_impact: An entire class of isolation features cannot be tested on the primary development VM.

pain_points.title: Testing the x86_64 plus NVIDIA boot path cheaply
pain_points.description: Container GPU clouds such as RunPod and Vast cannot boot a custom kernel or bootloader. GitHub GPU runners are paid, run GitHub's own images and require Team or Enterprise plans. Custom-image GPU VMs and bare-metal servers cost more and need automation.
pain_points.segment: Solo maintainers of bootable AI OS images
pain_points.evidence: GitHub's Linux 4-core GPU runner (Tesla T4, 16 GB) costs $0.052/min, and larger runners are always charged, even for public repositories. AWS g4dn.xlarge costs $0.526/hr on demand and $0.325/hr spot. Vast VMs must use docker.io/vastai/kvm images. RunPod lists only pod (container) products.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: GPU clouds optimize for ML containers rather than OS developers, and custom-image GPU capacity is concentrated in hyperscalers.
pain_points.current_solutions: Build AMIs with bootc-image-builder and boot them on spot g4dn or g6 instances. Use RunPod for userspace tests.
pain_points.quantified_impact: $0.33–0.62 per hour for custom-OS NVIDIA boot tests, against $3.12 per hour for GitHub GPU runners.

pain_points.title: The 16 GB unified memory ceiling
pain_points.description: By default macOS lets the GPU use about two thirds of RAM on machines with 32 GB or less, roughly 10.7 GB here. This limits local models to small dense models and fine-tuning to QLoRA on 8B or smaller.
pain_points.segment: Developers on 16 GB Apple Silicon
pain_points.evidence: The llama.cpp discussion shows the default reserve is 33.3% (25% above 32 GB), and iogpu.wired_limit_mb can raise the limit. Unsloth lists QLoRA minimums of 6 GB for 8B, 8.5 GB for 14B and 26 GB for 32B. gpt-oss-20b (21B total, 3.6B active, MXFP4) claims to run within 16 GB.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: This is a physical memory limit.
pain_points.current_solutions: Raise the wired limit with sysctl, quantize, and offload larger jobs to the cloud.
pain_points.quantified_impact: Roughly 10.7 GB is usable by the GPU by default.

pain_points.title: Hardware-matrix testing is heavy for small projects
pain_points.description: Proper multi-hardware OS testing tools such as openQA and LAVA need dedicated infrastructure. Small bootc projects such as the Universal Blue template provide only manual VM testing.
pain_points.segment: Small OS projects
pain_points.evidence: The ublue image-template offers just build-qcow2, run-vm-qcow2 and spawn-vm, with no automated boot tests. openQA tests full installs via VMs and screen checks and is used by openSUSE and Fedora. LAVA needs a multi-component server with workers.
pain_points.why_still_unsolved: Real hardware needs power control and console capture, which is costly to run.
pain_points.current_solutions: QEMU serial-console smoke tests in CI, plus community hardware reports.
pain_points.quantified_impact: Not quantified.

trends: Asahi has moved from feature work to upstreaming and M3. The GPU stack is conformant but performance work has slowed since the GPU lead left in August 2025.
GPU-in-microVM is maturing. DRM native context was merged into virglrenderer (Mesa 25.2), and libkrun supports Venus and native context. Lima 2.0 added a krunkit driver with a Venus Vulkan GPU.
Apple's own stack is pulling ahead for local inference. Ollama adopted MLX on Apple Silicon in 2026, which widens the gap over Linux Vulkan paths.
Vulkan-on-Metal translation is improving. LunarG's KosmicKrisp is a conformant Vulkan driver on Metal 4, but it needs macOS 26.
Apple's container tool iterates monthly (v1.2–1.5 between August and September 2026) and now includes Kubernetes commands, but offers no GPU support.
Image-based OS delivery (bootc plus GitHub Actions plus cosign) is the standard pattern for small distribution projects.
Free arm64 GitHub runners (since January 2025) make native aarch64 CI free for public repositories.

opportunities.idea: Make 'one microVM per agent with GPU access' an AgentOS primitive, built on libkrun or virtio-gpu (native context on Asahi and x86, Venus on macOS).
opportunities.why_now: Native context is upstream in virglrenderer (2025) and krunkit GPU support reached Lima 2.0 (2026). No distribution packages this pattern for agents.
opportunities.evidence: The Asahi 6.16 report says DRM native context was merged upstream. The libkrun README lists virtio-gpu with Venus and native context. Lima documents a krunkit driver with Venus.
opportunities.risk: Venus on macOS supports compute only. Nested virtualization is impossible on M1. The libkrun 2.0 API is unstable.

opportunities.idea: A hybrid development mode: run AgentOS in krunkit on macOS and route heavy inference to a host MLX or Metal server over an OpenAI-compatible socket.
opportunities.why_now: MLX on the host outperforms every Linux path on this hardware, and RamaLama already exposes both paths.
opportunities.evidence: Metal reaches 266 t/s prompt processing on an M1 Pro against about 38 t/s on Asahi Vulkan (base M1). krunkit reaches 74–80% of Metal.
opportunities.risk: This is a development crutch, not the shipped product. Users may confuse it with native performance.

opportunities.idea: Publish a reusable 'solo-maintainer OS CI' recipe: free GitHub x64 runners with KVM for QEMU boot smoke tests, plus spot g4dn AMI boot tests triggered per release.
opportunities.why_now: Small bootc projects lack automated boot tests, and spot T4 capacity costs about $0.33/hr.
opportunities.evidence: The ublue template offers only manual VM testing. GitHub KVM has been enabled on 2-vCPU runners since April 2024. g4dn.xlarge spot costs $0.325.
opportunities.risk: Spot capacity interruptions. AWS image import edge cases (ENA and NVMe drivers).

recommendations: Treat macOS on the M1 Pro as the primary daily loop. Build aarch64 bootc images in a Podman machine using the libkrun provider. Generate qcow2 or raw images with bootc-image-builder, then boot them in krunkit (Lima --vm-type=krunkit) for GPU Vulkan compute tests. Use UTM (QEMU with HVF) for installer ISO walkthroughs. Tooling cost: $0.

Run inference and fine-tuning experiments on the macOS host with MLX or llama.cpp Metal, and expose them to the guest over HTTP. Do not benchmark AgentOS performance on Asahi or in a VM and present those numbers as representative.

Dual-boot Fedora Asahi Remix 44 on the same M1 Pro, using about 80–100 GB of disk. Validate weekly: the 16K-page kernel, KVM-based agent sandboxes (impossible in a VM on M1), Vulkan llama.cpp, s2idle suspend and battery. Use the Asahi installer's 'UEFI environment only' option so that custom AgentOS images can boot from USB through U-Boot.

Ship two aarch64 kernel flavors: a generic 4K-page kernel for VMs and Arm clouds, and the Asahi 16K-page kernel for Mac bare metal. Consume Fedora Asahi kernel packages rather than maintaining a fork.

Make x86_64 plus NVIDIA the primary product target. In a public GitHub repository, use free ubuntu-latest runners (x64, KVM) to build images and run QEMU boot tests over a serial console. Use free ubuntu-24.04-arm runners for aarch64 builds.

For NVIDIA boot and driver validation, launch AWS g4dn.xlarge spot instances (about $0.33/hr, T4 16 GB) from bootc-image-builder AMIs at each release, with auto-termination through GitHub Actions and OIDC. Add g6.xlarge spot (about $0.62/hr, L4 24 GB) for newer driver branches.

Use RunPod community GPUs (RTX 3090 at $0.22/hr, RTX 4090 at $0.34/hr) only for userspace work: CUDA runtime, vLLM, and QLoRA jobs above 8B. Avoid GitHub GPU runners ($3.12/hr, paid plan, no custom OS).

Default model targets for 16 GB: 3–4B and 7–8B at Q4 (about 36 t/s on 7B Q4_0, M1 Pro 16-core, Metal). Use 14B Q4 only with a raised iogpu.wired_limit_mb and short context. Test gpt-oss-20b MXFP4 as a borderline case. Avoid 30B MoE models. Limit local fine-tuning to MLX QLoRA at 8B or below.
Ignore the Apple Neural Engine for AgentOS, because the driver is out of tree and has no LLM path.

Budget: $0 for tooling plus about $15–40 per month for cloud (roughly 20 spot GPU hours, storage and egress). Consider an optional one-time x86 plus NVIDIA test machine with KVM-over-IP for true bare-metal and Secure Boot testing. Its cost is unverified in this research, so get quotes first.
contrarian_signals: Bare-metal Linux on the M1 is slower for LLMs than a VM on macOS. Asahi Vulkan prompt processing is about 3x slower than Metal, while krunkit in a VM keeps 74–80% of Metal. A bootable OS on this specific hardware is therefore worse for AI than the host OS.
Developing mainly on Apple Silicon risks optimizing for a niche. Most production agent and fine-tuning workloads run on x86_64 with NVIDIA, which the M1 cannot test at all.
Asahi carries a bus-factor risk. Its founder resigned in February 2025 and its GPU lead left in August 2025. The GPU and DCP drivers were still described as too large to upstream in August 2026.

Secondary sources conflict with primary ones. One 2026 blog lists Vulkan 1.3 and no VP9/HEVC decode, while primary sources report Vulkan 1.4 conformance and mostly reliable AVC/HEVC/VP9 decode. Rely on asahilinux.org and maintainer posts only.
On M1 hardware, the Lima nested-virtualization statement conflicts with the stated goal of safe agent sandboxing tested in VMs.

Red Hat's krunkit benchmark was run on an M4 Pro with 48 GB, so the ratio may not hold on an M1 Pro with 16 GB. The 2024 design note set an 8 GB GPU memory cap, and whether it was lifted is unverified.
The research itself is limited: the shared WebSearch budget ran out after 3 searches, so pricing for Hetzner, GCP and Vultr and some 2026 status claims could not be confirmed.
open_questions: Has the 8 GB GPU memory limit in krunkit/Venus been lifted, and how does performance compare on an M1 Pro with 16 GB?
Has Asahi Vulkan (Honeykrisp) performance for llama.cpp improved in Mesa 25.x or 26.x? Measure pp512 and tg128 on this exact M1 Pro.
What is Hetzner GEX45's current monthly and hourly price, and can it boot a custom ISO through the VNC installer or KVM console?
Was Equinix Metal sunset in June 2026 as previously announced? Verification failed (HTTP 403).
Will Rosetta for Linux VMs survive Apple's announced Rosetta phase-out after macOS 27? This affects x86_64 userspace testing on the Mac.
Does Fedora Asahi Remix support bootc or atomic variants well enough to share one AgentOS image pipeline across Mac and x86?
Do GitHub's free ubuntu-24.04-arm runners expose /dev/kvm for aarch64 boot tests?

checks.claim: Founder commit concentration: Open WebUI 13,393 of 19,511 (68.6%), Coolify 13,153 of 17,846 (73.7%), Omarchy 4,829 of 7,026 (68.7%), Bazzite 5,693 of 8,613 (66.1%), Pinokio 677 of 677, llama.cpp 2,032 of 11,691 (17.4%). The brief infers that gaining contributors did not lift the founder's load, and recommends expecting to write 70% or more of commits.
checks.corrected_statement: The counts reproduce exactly (llama.cpp now shows 11,693 commits). Commit counts mostly measure how often each person commits, not how much work they do. Open WebUI's founder made 100 commits between 12 and 14 Oct 2026, and DHH made 100 between 11 and 14 Oct. The data show concentration. They do not show that contributors failed to reduce load, and Coolify's paid hire, with 1,858 commits, did take on real work.
checks.evidence: GitHub API queries on 16 Oct 2026 (authenticated gh and unauthenticated curl) reproduced every star count and contributor count. Merge commits do not inflate the founder shares: they were 2 of tjbck's last 100 commits, 3 of andrasbacsai's, 0 of dhh's and 0 of ggerganov's. Founders still wrote most recent commits: 92 of Coolify's last 100 and 81 of Omarchy's last 100. Omarchy has 5,458 open items (2,250 issues and 3,208 PRs), which supports the review-burden point but was not cited in the brief.

checks.claim: Ollama has raised USD 88M (blog, 9 Jul 2026) and introduced per-token pricing (31 Aug 2026); it claims 8.9 million developers and use by 85% of the Fortune 500.
checks.corrected_statement: Ollama announced USD 88M from Benchmark, Theory Ventures and 8VC on 9 Jul 2026, without naming the round. On 31 Aug 2026, Ollama moved its cloud Pro, Max and Team plans to per-token pricing, and existing subscribers keep their current plans until they change tier. The announcement does not cover local use. The 8.9M developer and 85% Fortune 500 figures are self-reported and undefined.
checks.evidence: The July post quotes the USD 88M raise and names the investors. The 31 Aug post says that Pro, Max and Team plans 'now use transparent per-token pricing.' The July post also contrasts local models with 'runaway per-token bills', so the pricing change applies to the cloud only.

checks.claim: Exit via acquisition: ggml joined Hugging Face (20 Feb 2026) and Astral was acquired by OpenAI (March 2026); the brief's trend and recommendation sections rely on these as completed acquisitions.
checks.corrected_statement: Hugging Face announced on 20 Feb 2026 that ggml.ai was joining it. The team keeps '100%' of its time on llama.cpp with 'full autonomy'. No financial terms, licence or governance mechanism were stated. On 19 Mar 2026, Astral said it had 'entered into an agreement to join' OpenAI. The page does not confirm that the deal has closed, and treating it as a completed acquisition is not supported by the source.
checks.evidence: The Hugging Face post confirms the date and the autonomy wording, and promises to make llama.cpp 'ubiquitous and readily available everywhere'. It does not mention whisper.cpp. The Astral post confirms the date and the claim of 'hundreds of millions of downloads per month'. It describes joining Codex as a future step and gives no closing conditions or licence statement.

checks.claim: Funding recommendation: apply to NLnet's next call (3 Nov 2026 deadline) for an agent-sandbox component; NGI Zero Commons final call closed 1 Jun 2026, calls paused 12 Jun 2026, first grants EUR 5,000-50,000; Sovereign Tech Fund requires cost above EUR 50,000, about 6 months, no prototypes, OSI/FSF licence.
checks.corrected_statement: The individual facts are correct, but the recommendation does not fit. NLnet's Restack call (deadline 3 Nov 2026, EUR 5k-50k) says 'AI-related projects are not within scope' unless they already have more than 1 million active human users. It also requires a strong European dimension: normally, team members in Horizon Europe-eligible countries receive at least 60% of the funds, and other proposals are considered only as exceptions. CodeSupply funds software supply-chain metadata only. An agent-sandbox application from a founder outside Europe is therefore unlikely to qualify unless the project is reframed as non-AI security infrastructure and has European participation. The Sovereign Tech Fund terms are confirmed.
checks.evidence: The NLnet Commons Fund page states that the 'thirteenth and final call... closed on June 1st 2026' and that grants run EUR 5,000-50,000 from a EUR 21.6M budget. The news page lists the 12 Jun 2026 pause notice, the 3 Aug 2026 move to odd-month deadlines and the 3 Sep 2026 call for 3 Nov. The Restack scope and eligibility pages contain the AI exclusion and the European-dimension rule. The Sovereign Tech Fund page states that costs 'must exceed EUR 50,000', the process takes about six months, it does not fund prototypes, it is not seeking user-facing applications, and code must use an OSI or FSF licence.

checks.claim: Recommendation: build AgentOS as a Containerfile FROM a Fedora bootc or Universal Blue base using the ublue-os image-template, and develop and test the aarch64 image in a VM on the M1 Pro.
checks.corrected_statement: The Universal Blue route and the aarch64 plan conflict. As of 16 Oct 2026, the Universal Blue images (base-main, bazzite, bluefin and aurora) are amd64 only, and the image-template's default base is bazzite:stable (amd64). Only Fedora's own bootc image (quay.io/fedora/fedora-bootc:44) is multi-architecture and includes arm64. An aarch64 build developed on an M1 Pro must therefore start FROM fedora-bootc, not a Universal Blue image, or depend on slow amd64 emulation. The template's disk-build workflow does support arm64 runners.
checks.evidence: Image configs fetched from GHCR give architecture 'amd64' for ublue-os/bazzite:stable, bluefin:stable and base-main:latest. The bluefin:lts index lists only amd64. The Quay manifest list for fedora/fedora-bootc:44 lists arm64, ppc64le, s390x and amd64. The image-template Containerfile starts 'FROM ghcr.io/ublue-os/bazzite:stable', and build-disk.yml offers amd64 and arm64 platforms.

checks.claim: Asahi Linux does not yet support M3/M4 (M3/M4 support deferred), so bare-metal Apple Silicon is a narrowing target and hardware-level OS work is the documented burnout path.
checks.corrected_statement: Asahi Linux announced official installer support for M3, M3 Pro and M3 Max MacBooks and iMacs on 6 Sep 2026, and on 15 Sep 2026 stopped requiring expert mode. GPU acceleration is not yet usable on M3, the M3 Ultra is unsupported, and sleep and HDMI do not work. M4 and M5 remain unsupported. Since the leadership change the project has also upstreamed its Mesa drivers (Aug 2025) and its SMC drivers (Oct-Dec 2025). The burnout of the founder is accurate, but the claim that the project stalled is outdated.
checks.evidence: The Asahi blog lists 'M2: Episode 1 (or, Asahi Linux on M3)', which states that Asahi Linux 'now officially supports Macs with an M3 series SoC'. The same blog has progress reports for Linux 6.14 through 7.2. The resignation post's May 2026 update confirms that Martin has left the community entirely.

checks.claim: Asahi's Open Collective raised about USD 156,000 in roughly 20 months for a seven-person team, showing donations do not fund an OS.
checks.corrected_statement: The page reports USD 156,337.62 raised, USD 117,653.87 as the estimated annual budget, 967 contributors and seven listed team members. Only USD 43,419.98 has been disbursed, leaving a balance of USD 112,917.64, so the collective is not paying salaries to seven people. The collective began in February 2025, when the founder redirected his personal Patreon and GitHub Sponsors income to it. Its totals therefore exclude years of earlier personal-channel funding and cannot by themselves show that donations decay.
checks.evidence: The Open Collective page gives the totals, the disbursed amount and the balance, and its earliest contributions date from February 2025. The resignation post says the author is pausing his Patreon and asks supporters to redirect funding to the OpenCollective. It also states that donation volume peaked in the first month or two and then kept slowly decreasing.

checks.claim: Open WebUI branding clause effective v0.6.6 (19 Apr 2025), 50-user threshold, not OSI-approved, CLA after v0.6.5; Jan moved AGPL to Apache 2.0 in May 2025.
checks.corrected_statement: Both licence facts are confirmed. Open WebUI's page states that 'v0.6.6+ is not an OSI-approved' licence and that code up to v0.6.5 remains BSD-3-Clause. Jan's LICENSE was changed to Apache on 20 May 2025 (PR #5042), but GitHub still reports Jan's licence as NOASSERTION, so its LICENSE file contains more than the standard Apache text.
checks.evidence: The Open WebUI licence page gives the v0.6.6 effective date and the 50-user, 30-day threshold, and says the CLA applies from v0.6.6. Its TL;DR and body word the threshold slightly differently. The janhq/jan LICENSE commit history shows 'Jan's code is now under the Apache license (#5042)' dated 2025-05-20.

checks.claim: Omarchy self-reports 1,280,643 ISO downloads in year one, USD 23.65M pledged to the Omacom Foundation, a USD 100,000 bug bounty, and markets itself as 'The malleable OS for the age of agents' without sandboxing claims.
checks.corrected_statement: The homepage reports these figures. All are self-reported, pledges are not receipts, and the page gives no breakdown that adds up to USD 23.65M. OpenAI is also listed as a corporate patron, in addition to Meta Superintelligence Labs, DigitalOcean and Alibaba Cloud. The page describes no sandboxing, permissions or rollback.
checks.evidence: omarchy.org quotes the download count, pledge total and bounty fund, the bounties are administered through HackerOne, and the page lists its patron tiers.

missed_counter_evidence: NLnet's Restack call, the main 3 Nov 2026 option, excludes AI-related projects unless they already have more than 1 million active users, and normally requires 60% of funds to go to team members in Horizon Europe-eligible countries. The brief left eligibility outside the EU as an open question, but this rule directly undermines its NLnet recommendation.

Universal Blue images (base-main, bazzite, bluefin, aurora) are amd64 only as of 16 Oct 2026. Only quay.io/fedora/fedora-bootc:44 provides arm64, so 'FROM Universal Blue' and 'test aarch64 on the M1 Pro' cannot both apply.

Asahi Linux officially supports M3, M3 Pro and M3 Max installs since September 2026 (without GPU acceleration), and has upstreamed its Mesa and SMC drivers since the founder left. The brief's statement that Asahi does not support M3 is outdated. The M1 Pro remains Asahi's best-supported generation, so a bare-metal aarch64 test target is available alongside VMs.

Ollama added an MLX engine for Apple Silicon (preview 30 Mar 2026, performance update 11 Jun 2026), and Ollama 0.30 added GGUF support through llama.cpp (5 Jun 2026). This matters to an M1 Pro developer: native macOS inference is now strong, while Linux VMs on the same machine have no Metal access. The brief's open question about GPU in VMs should be weighed against this.

curl's bug-bounty page now states that there is no bug bounty, so the brief's 'considering removal of bounties' is out of date. In October 2026, curl also credited the AI-assisted Aisle audit with 35 published CVEs and acknowledged an Anthropic-found use-after-free that became remote code execution. A policy that requires disclosure of AI use is more defensible than an anti-AI policy.
Omarchy's own backlog is 5,458 open items (2,250 issues and 3,208 PRs), which is stronger review-burden evidence than the Ollama, Bazzite and Pinokio figures the brief cited.

Asahi's Open Collective has disbursed only USD 43,420 of USD 156,338, so unspent funds, not only low donations, limit how far the money goes. The brief presents the total as if it funds seven developers.
The Astral announcement describes an agreement, not a completed deal, and Hugging Face describes ggml as 'joining'. Neither discloses terms, so calling both 'acquisitions' overstates the record.
Minor: Simon Willison ran llama.cpp the night it was released (10 Mar 2023), not one day later.
verify:oss_solo_sustainability.reliability_note: Summary: the brief's numbers are highly accurate, but some recommendations rest on facts it never checked or that are now out of date. Every GitHub star, commit and contributor figure, and every figure from Ollama, Omarchy, Open WebUI, the Sovereign Tech Fund and NLnet, matched the primary sources on 16 Oct 2026. The weaker parts are interpretive or practical. Commit counts are treated as workload. Astral and ggml are presented as completed acquisitions. Asahi's M3 status is out of date. The NLnet recommendation ignores Restack's exclusion of AI projects and its European-dimension rule. The bootc recommendation pairs amd64-only Universal Blue bases with aarch64 development on an M1 Pro. Method: web search was unavailable because the shared budget was exhausted, so all checks used direct fetches of primary pages and live GitHub, GHCR and Quay API queries. Some findings, such as whether the Astral deal closed and how Restack eligibility applies outside Europe, remain unconfirmed and need a follow-up search. Two questions for the orchestrator: does the founder have European collaborators who could meet the NLnet rule, and is x86_64 with NVIDIA, rather than aarch64, the real v0.1 target?

checks.claim: Bluefin GDX already ships CentOS Stream 10 with NVIDIA drivers, CUDA, RamaLama and uv on x86_64 and aarch64 with Secure Boot, and Bluefin LTS/GDX keep kernel 6.12 for the release lifetime. The brief uses this as the reference model behind its CentOS Stream 10 recommendation.
checks.corrected_statement: The September 2025 description is out of date. GDX moved to the Fedora CoreOS (HWE) kernel on 11 Jan 2026. In July 2026 Project Bluefin announced that GDX would stop being a separate image and become a userspace mode, with CUDA delivered through containers, and that LTS would move entirely onto Fedora kernels. Project Bluefin's own LTS repository was later rebranded Uranium (thallium-suite / quill-oci), and that repository was archived on 15 Oct 2026. Only the legacy ublue-os/bluefin-lts repository still builds GDX, for amd64 and arm64. It does this with a Fedora CoreOS kernel and Fedora NVIDIA packages from negativo17 on top of CentOS userspace. Current Secure Boot status for GDX was not verified.
checks.evidence: Sources checked: the GitHub API, the ublue-os/bluefin-lts Justfile, and the projectbluefin blog. In the Justfile, gdx=1 sets AKMODS_BASE=coreos-stable-43. The kernel-swap.sh history includes 'fix: switch GDX to HWE kernel (#1007)', merged 2026-01-11. The GDX script 20-nvidia.sh installs nvidia-driver-cuda from negativo17's fedora-nvidia repository. The Project Bluefin blog post of 2 Jul 2026 says DX and GDX images are merged, GDX moves to 'ujust aimode', CUDA can be consumed through containers, and everything is consolidated onto Fedora's kernels. It gives the reason that GitHub runners lacked the space and resources for GDX. The quill-oci/uranium repository shows archived=true, last pushed 2026-10-15, with the commit 'bump kernel version to 7.2.5 from fedore core os'. The legacy GDX workflow last succeeded on 2026-10-15.
