Bluefin LTS and GDX GA post

checks.claim: bootc 1.17.0 (6 Oct) declared its composefs backend stable, and its CLI and API are stable.
checks.corrected_statement: bootc v1.17.0, published 2026-10-06T18:15:02Z, declares the composefs backend stable and calls the 'core on-disk format' ready for production. ostree is still the default backend. The composefs known-issues list says logically bound images are not implemented, there is no in-place move from an ostree system, and upgrades of UKI installs from other releases are not yet tested. The statement that the CLI and API are stable comes from the bootc docs, not from this release, and it covers surface APIs only. bootc is still a CNCF Sandbox project.
checks.evidence: The GitHub releases API shows published_at 2026-10-06T18:15:02Z, which settles the brief's uncertainty about the year. The release body says 'This release declares the composefs backend as stable.' The bootc-composefs(7) page says the backend 'is stable', but it also lists logically bound images as not implemented, notes the missing ostree-to-composefs transition, and lists unimplemented commands (bootc edit, install reset). The bootc docs say the CLI and API are 'considered stable' and that this 'refers to the surface APIs'. The CNCF lists bootc as Sandbox (accepted 21 Jan 2025). This creates a conflict in the brief: it recommends logically bound images, but the composefs or sealed path it plans to adopt later does not support them yet.

checks.claim: Bazzite, built the Universal Blue way, passed 100,000 weekly active devices (15 Oct 2026).
checks.corrected_statement: Confirmed. Universal Blue's own countme badge shows Bazzite at '100k', and the project charts this as 'Weekly Active Devices' from Fedora DNF countme data. The founder's post calls them 'users'. Bazzite is Fedora Kinoite-based and mostly x86_64. The same dataset puts the CentOS-based Bluefin LTS at 64, Bluefin at 4.1k and Aurora at 3.1k. The scale proof therefore applies to the Fedora path, not to the CentOS Stream 10 base the brief recommends.
checks.evidence: GamingOnLinux, 15 Oct 2026, quotes founder Kyle Gospodnetich: 'passed 100,000 weekly active users'. The ublue-os/countme badge-endpoints/bazzite.json file reads message '100k' (updated 2026-10-08), and the plot title in countme.py is 'Weekly Active Devices'. A code comment in data_processing.py says Bluefin LTS data 'is not gathered from fedora repos', so the LTS figure may be undercounted. The Bazzite Containerfile builds FROM ublue-os/kinoite-main with akmods, and the akmods Fedora main and ogc targets are x86_64 only.

sources.title: Bazzite continues growing, now with over 100k weekly active devices

checks.claim: GitHub gives public repositories free x64 and arm64 runners (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 14 GB SSD), so x86_64 and aarch64 images can both be built for free in CI.
checks.corrected_statement: Confirmed. Standard Linux runners for public repositories are 4 CPU, 16 GB RAM and 14 GB SSD, for both x64 (ubuntu-24.04, ubuntu-26.04) and arm64 (ubuntu-24.04-arm, ubuntu-26.04-arm). GitHub states that usage is free for public repositories on standard runners, and that larger runners are always charged. Being free does not make them big enough: Project Bluefin reported in July 2026 that these runners lacked the space and resources for its CUDA-bearing GDX image.
checks.evidence: The GitHub-hosted runners reference table lists 'Linux 4 16 GB 14 GB' for both x64 and arm64. The billing docs say: 'GitHub Actions usage is free for self-hosted runners and for public repositories that use standard GitHub-hosted runners.' The runner docs do not say whether KVM or nested virtualisation is available on Linux runners, so that remains unverified. The Bluefin LTS reusable workflow builds amd64 on ubuntu-24.04 and arm64 on ubuntu-24.04-arm, and includes a 'Maximize build space' step.

checks.claim: AMD lists RHEL 10.x as supported for ROCm, but not Fedora or NixOS, which favours a RHEL-family base; a CentOS Stream 10 base matches the RHEL 10 support listed by NVIDIA and ROCm.
checks.corrected_statement: Fedora and NixOS are indeed absent from ROCm's support list. CentOS Stream and AlmaLinux are absent too, so a CentOS Stream 10 base is not officially supported either. The brief's source (dated 2026-07-15, ROCm 7.14 era) has been replaced by ROCm Core SDK 10.1.0, released 2026-10-05 and built with TheRock. That release lists RHEL 10.2, 10.0, 9.8, 9.6, 9.4 and 8.10, plus Ubuntu 26.04.1, 24.04.5 and 22.04.5, SLES 16.0 and 15.7, Debian, Oracle Linux and Rocky 9. Consumer Radeon support is limited to Ubuntu and selected RHEL releases. An image that swaps in a Fedora CoreOS kernel, as Bluefin LTS now does, gives up any RHEL kernel alignment.
checks.evidence: The system-requirements page (dated 2026-07-15) lists RHEL 10.1, 10.0, 9.7, 9.6, 9.4 and 8.10, but not Fedora, CentOS Stream or AlmaLinux. It limits Radeon and Radeon PRO to Ubuntu 24.04.4, 22.04.5, RHEL 10.1 and 9.7, and carries a banner saying it has moved to the compatibility matrix. That matrix and the release notes show ROCm 10.1.0 (2026-10-05) with the newer distribution list. Neither page explains the jump from 7.x to 10.x, beyond noting that 'Since ROCm 7.14, ROCm uses TheRock'.

missed_counter_evidence: Project Bluefin restructured in July 2026. DX and GDX images were merged, AI and CUDA tooling moved to a userspace 'ujust aimode' with CUDA through containers, signing moved to keyless OIDC, and layers are now built with chunkah. This matches the brief's advice to keep CUDA out of /usr, but it removes the GDX reference image the brief relies on.

Bluefin LTS was renamed Uranium under thallium-suite / quill-oci (the quill-oci organisation was created 12 Oct 2026), and that repository was archived on 15 Oct 2026. The README says Uranium 'has no community infrastructure of its own yet'. A CentOS-based downstream maintained by a tiny team turns out to be organisationally fragile.

Project Bluefin is moving its effort to new bases. Dakota is GNOME OS built with BuildStream (alpha). Utah is built on Fedora Hummingbird (pre-alpha, nothing published). Bluefin Server, announced in Sep 2026, is a freedesktop-sdk, DDI-first OS with signed UKIs, a dm-verity /usr and systemd-sysupdate (alpha). These are important references for the verified-boot design and a sign that the reference team is leaving CentOS Stream.

Universal Blue already runs a CentOS 10 NVIDIA module pipeline (Bluefin LTS mounts ghcr.io/ublue-os/akmods-nvidia-open:centos-10). This answers the brief's open question. The kernel and modules are signed with Universal Blue's shared key, so the founder would either depend on that key or run their own pipeline.

The ublue-os/akmods nvidia-open builds for the Fedora main and ogc flavours (44 and 45) are x86_64 only. aarch64 NVIDIA modules exist only for the coreos-stable flavours, which affects the plan for an aarch64 agentos-nvidia image.

The brief cited the Nix CUDA cache thread selectively. A follow-up post on 17 Dec 2025 said Flox caches stable channels. Flox's documentation shows stable (monthly) and lts (six-monthly) cadence branches of its own fork. Release channels are still not built, so 'no cache for stable releases' is broadly accurate but overstated.

Universal Blue's countme data puts Bluefin LTS at 64 active users, against 4.1k for Bluefin and 100k for Bazzite. The data may undercount CentOS hits, but it does not support the claim that a tiny team ships at scale on a CentOS Stream 10 base.
ROCm 10.1.0 (5 Oct 2026) adds Ubuntu 26.04.1 and SLES 16 and is built with TheRock. The brief's ROCm version details and its vLLM ROCm wheel claims (ROCm 7.0 and 7.2.1) are probably out of date.

Because the bootc composefs backend has no logically bound images and no in-place move from ostree, a system installed today on the default ostree backend has to be reinstalled to adopt composefs or sealed images later. The brief's advice to 'postpone measured boot' therefore carries a reinstall cost.
verify:bootable_tooling.reliability_note: Summary: the brief's dated facts mostly hold, but its central reference model is out of date. Bluefin GDX, as an image with kernel 6.12 for the release lifetime, was retired or restructured in 2026, and the LTS line has been spun out and archived. That weakens the claim that CentOS Stream 10 is the 'only base that meets all four needs'. Method: the shared web-search budget ran out on the first query, so all verification used direct fetches of primary documents and read-only GitHub API calls. A small model summarised the WebFetch pages, so quoted wording should be spot-checked; the ROCm 10.1.0 version jump in particular is unexplained by AMD. Discourse pages for Universal Blue returned HTTP 403. Clarifying questions for the founder: (1) Does AgentOS need RHEL-kernel ABI stability at all, given that upstream Bluefin abandoned the 6.12 kernel for lack of users? (2) Is a Fedora-based bootc image, which carries the 100k-device evidence, acceptable if ROCm and NVIDIA run only in containers?

checks.claim: No product yet treats agents as first-class OS principals; no distro offers OS-level, per-agent controls over filesystem, network, credentials or approvals (executive summary and the first pain point).
checks.corrected_statement: No mainstream Linux distribution was found that ships per-agent OS identities by default. Microsoft Windows 11, however, has offered agent accounts and an agent workspace in preview since October to December 2025. Each agent gets its own account and a separate Windows session, and Windows asks for consent per agent and per known folder. The claim holds only if it is limited to Linux, and it should be worded that way.
checks.evidence: The Microsoft support page 'Experimental agentic features' says each agent operates using its own account, distinct from the user's personal account, and that the agent workspace runs in a separate Windows session. The default for known folders (Documents, Downloads, Desktop and so on) is to ask for consent, with options 'Allow Always', 'Ask every time' and 'Never allow'. The page was first published on 2025-10-16 and updated on 2025-11-17 and 2025-12-05 (preview builds 26100.7344+ and 26220.7262+). The feature is off by default and is still in preview. NVIDIA OpenShell also now ships an MXC compute driver that runs agents in Windows AppContainer or isolation sessions (Windows 11 Insider build 26300.8553 or later). I could not run a search for Linux counterexamples because the web search budget was used up.

checks.claim: Omarchy has 44,921 stars, 1.28M year-one ISO downloads and $23.65M pledged, calls itself 'agentic', and its launcher starts every coding agent with its permission prompts switched off.
checks.corrected_statement: The adoption figures and the 'agentic' label are correct. However, omarchy-agent does not switch off permissions for every agent. Of its 15 agent entries, 11 pass skip or auto-approve flags (opencode --auto, agy --dangerously-skip-permissions, copilot --allow-all, crush --yolo, grok --permission-mode bypassPermissions, codex --approve-for-me, cursor-agent --yolo --trust, hermes --yolo, muse --approval-mode never, omp --auto-approve, kimi --yolo). Claude is launched in auto mode, which is classifier-reviewed and is Claude Code's own built-in default, not a bypass. OpenClaw, Pi and Ori get no skip flag. Muse keeps its own sandbox.
checks.evidence: The GitHub API returns 44,921 stars, 5,493 forks, MIT licence and repository creation on 2025-06-01. The default branch is 'quattro', not master. omarchy.org says 'Beautiful, fun & agentic Linux', offers version 4.0.4, and reports 1,280,643 year-one ISO downloads and $23,650,000 pledged. It offers Apple Silicon only through a VM. The raw script on the quattro branch shows 'claude --permission-mode auto'. Its comment states that agents launched from the keybinding or menu run unattended. Claude Code documentation says that in auto mode a classifier reviews actions instead of the user, and that auto mode is the built-in starting mode in v2.1.283 or later. bypassPermissions is a separate mode, intended for isolated containers and VMs.

checks.claim: OpenClaw has 722 published GitHub security advisories in 2026 (14 critical, 249 high, 390 medium, 69 low), 'January to September', 'about 9 months'; 392k stars.
checks.corrected_statement: Confirmed exactly: 722 published advisories (14 critical, 249 high, 390 medium, 69 low) and 392,136 stars. The advisories run from 2026-01-31 to 2026-09-11, about 7.4 months rather than 9. They are heavily front-loaded: 424 of 722 (59 percent) were published in February and March, none in July or August, and 75 in September. The count reflects a disclosure wave after launch, not a steady monthly rate.
checks.evidence: I paginated the GitHub REST API (security-advisories, state=published, cursor pagination) and found 722 unique GHSA IDs. Severity counts: medium 390, high 249, low 69, critical 14. Advisories by month: January 3, February 220, March 204, April 108, May 67, June 45, September 75. The web UI shows 73 pages, with only 2 entries on the last page. The repository was created on 2025-11-24.

checks.claim: NVIDIA OpenShell is alpha, needs Docker or Podman, does not specify its isolation mechanisms in the docs, and has telemetry on by default; the founder should contribute an OS-native, non-Docker driver.
checks.corrected_statement: OpenShell is no longer labelled alpha. It is on a 0.1.x 'stable release cadence', with v0.1.4 released on 2026-10-13. NemoClaw is still alpha. OpenShell documents its kernel mechanisms in detail: Landlock LSM (ABI 3, Linux 6.2 or later, required), seccomp BPF and seccomp user notification, a dedicated network namespace with a veth pair, and privilege drop through setuid and setgid. It does not need Docker. A libkrun MicroVM driver runs on KVM (Linux) and Hypervisor.framework (macOS), alongside Docker, Podman, Kubernetes and a Windows MXC driver. Telemetry is on by default, with an opt-out. A non-Docker driver therefore already exists, so the recommendation should change from 'contribute one' to 'evaluate the MicroVM driver and a host-native driver'.
checks.evidence: The README says 'New in OpenShell 0.1.x: a stable release cadence, new isolation primitives' and lists the requirement as 'Docker, Podman, or host virtualization'. docs/about/support-matrix.mdx lists Landlock and seccomp as Required and marks MicroVM as 'Supported for VM-backed sandboxes'. It also says that on macOS these kernel modules run inside the Docker Desktop Linux VM. docs/security/best-practices.mdx names the Landlock LSM, Seccomp BPF and 'Network Namespace Isolation'. The source contains crates/openshell-sandbox/src/linux/landlock.rs and seccomp.rs. The VM driver README is labelled 'Status: Experimental', which does not match the support matrix. The GitHub API shows 16,376 stars and Apache-2.0.

checks.claim: DGX Spark runs DGX OS 7.5.0 (kernel 6.17, driver 580.159.03, CUDA 13.0.2). NVIDIA admits that nvidia-smi shows memory as 'Not Supported' and that cudaMemGetInfo under-reports. The workaround is MemAvailable/SwapFree estimation or drop_caches. The July 2026 release improved OOM handling.
checks.corrected_statement: Confirmed, with framing caveats. NVIDIA describes the nvidia-smi 'Memory-Usage: Not Supported' output as expected behaviour on iGPU platforms, not as a defect. cudaMemGetInfo omits memory that could be reclaimed from swap. NVIDIA labels drop_caches as a workaround for debugging only. The July 2026 release adds better OOM handling and a BIOS option that reserves 2 GB (default) or 4 GB for the display. No release after July 2026 is listed. The software versions apply to the Founders Edition, and partner GB10 systems may lag.
checks.evidence: The Known Issues page was last updated on Sep 10, 2026. It contains sample C code that parses MemAvailable and SwapFree from /proc/meminfo, and the code treats free swap as zero when huge pages are configured. The Release Notes list releases from November 2025 to July 2026, identify 7.5.0 as current, and give 580.159.03, CUDA 13.0.2 and Canonical kernel 6.17 in the version table. The table is not explicitly tied to the July release.

missed_counter_evidence: Windows 11 agent accounts and agent workspace (preview since October to December 2025) already give each agent its own OS account, a separate session and per-folder consent. A major OS vendor has therefore already started the 'agents as OS principals' idea, which weakens the novelty of the headline.

Agent CLIs are building OS-enforced sandboxing into themselves. Claude Code's built-in Bash sandbox uses Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap plus socat (optional seccomp) on Linux and WSL2, with a domain-allowlist proxy, and classifier-reviewed auto mode became its default in v2.1.283. This competes directly with the proposed 'agentd' broker.

OpenShell already provides the non-Docker path the brief recommends building: a libkrun MicroVM driver (KVM and Hypervisor.framework), a Kubernetes driver with user namespaces, and a Microsoft MXC/AppContainer driver for Windows 11 Insider builds. It also ships a formal policy prover. Four tagged releases (v0.1.1 to v0.1.4) came out between 2026-09-26 and 2026-10-13.

On macOS, OpenShell enforces Landlock and seccomp inside the Docker Desktop Linux VM. A Linux kernel boundary is still required, but delivering a Linux VM image may be enough. This supports a 'Linux image' strategy more than a natively booted OS.

OpenClaw advisories peaked in February and March 2026 (59 percent of all), with none published in July or August. Using '722 advisories' as evidence of an ongoing risk rate overstates the current trend.
Fedora Asahi Remix officially supports only M1 and M2 series devices. M3 appears only in feature tables, and M4 is not mentioned. The brief's 'M3 listed in device tables' could be misread as support.
Inconsistency inside OpenShell: the VM driver README says 'Experimental', while the support matrix says 'Supported'. The founder should treat VM-backed isolation as experimental.

The founder should answer two questions before relying on this brief. Is the target strictly Linux, or does Windows agent-workspace competition matter? Would an OpenShell-based Linux VM image meet the 'bootable OS' goal?
verify:existing_ai_distros.reliability_note: Executive summary: of the five claims checked, two are confirmed (OpenClaw advisories, DGX Spark memory issues), one is partially confirmed (Omarchy), one is disputed (the 'no OS treats agents as principals' headline) and one is refuted (OpenShell maturity and documentation). The brief's numbers are highly accurate: GitHub API values for Omarchy, OpenClaw, NemoClaw, OpenShell, inference-snaps and InstructLab matched exactly or within one star. The quoted wording from RHEL AI 3.5 ('NVIDIA CUDA and AMD ROCm AI accelerators only', a bootc image) and from the DGX Spark docs was verified. The weaknesses are qualitative. The brief overstates Omarchy's permission bypass by counting Claude's default auto mode as a bypass. Its description of OpenShell is out of date: the project is not alpha, does document Landlock, seccomp and netns, and does not need Docker. It also misses Windows 11 agent accounts, which undercut the headline. Recommendations that depend on OpenShell (contribute a non-Docker driver, verify its kernel mechanisms) should be revised. Limitation: the shared web search budget was used up after one attempted search, so all checks used direct primary-source fetches and the GitHub API. Linux-specific counterexamples to the headline, Ubuntu 26.04 AI features and newer Omarchy sandboxing work were not searched. A follow-up message would allow those searches to continue.

checks.claim: AIOS is effectively dormant: its last tagged release is v0.2.2 from March 2025 (2025-03-12), with 6.5k stars and no 2026 activity. The brief uses this as a contrarian signal.
checks.corrected_statement: AIOS published v0.3.0 on 2026-01-22. The tag was created 2025-11-24, and GitHub marks it 'Latest'. v0.2.2 was published on 2025-03-08, not 2025-03-12; the 03-12 date comes from the README news list. Commits continued until 2026-07-20, including per-user memory isolation work. The repository has 6,478 stars. Two claims hold: the README news list has no 2026 items, and the Rust rewrite (aios-rs) has placeholder code only and says it is 'NOT feature-parity yet'.
checks.evidence: The GitHub releases API lists v0.3.0 published 2026-01-22T14:07:28Z and v0.2.2 published 2025-03-08T17:11:40Z. The repository API shows 6,478 stars and a last push on 2026-07-20. The v0.3.0 notes include an MCP computer-use environment, Qdrant support and the aios-rs scaffold. The README still calls AIOS 'an abstraction layer over the operating system kernel', so the claim that it runs in userland is correct.

checks.claim: Landlock has reached ABI 11 (UDP rules, TSYNC). The recommendation sets a kernel floor of Linux 6.15 (Landlock audit) so the OS image can use these features.
checks.corrected_statement:
ABI 11 appears only in Linux 7.3-rc, which was unreleased on 2026-10-16 (the latest tag is v7.3-rc7). ABI 11 adds LANDLOCK_RESTRICT_SELF_NO_NEW_PRIVS, not UDP or TSYNC. The mapping is:
- Linux 6.15 to 6.19: ABI 7 (audit).
- Linux 7.0: ABI 8 (TSYNC).
- Linux 7.1: ABI 9 (pathname Unix socket control, FS_RESOLVE_UNIX).
- Linux 7.2: ABI 10 (UDP).
A 6.15 floor therefore gives neither UDP rules nor TSYNC. The floor must be at least 7.2 for UDP and 7.3 for ABI 11.
checks.evidence: In kernel source, security/landlock/syscalls.c sets landlock_abi_version to 7 at v6.15, v6.16, v6.18 and v6.19. It is 8 at v7.0, 9 at v7.1, 10 at v7.2 and 11 at v7.3-rc7. The docs.kernel.org page is built from 7.3.0-rc7. It lists TSYNC under ABI 8, UDP under ABI 10 and NO_NEW_PRIVS under ABI 11, and it does not map ABIs to kernel releases. The landlock.io news page stops at 6.15. This resolves the brief's open question about which kernels carry ABIs 8 to 11.

checks.claim: The Claude Code sandbox covers shell commands only. MCP servers, hooks and LSP servers run with full access, an unsandboxed retry exists, and docker is incompatible. Anthropic reports 84% fewer permission prompts.
checks.corrected_statement:
Confirmed, with three omissions:
- The sandbox is off by default.
- The retry can be disabled with allowUnsandboxedCommands:false, and failIfUnavailable stops unsandboxed fallback. On Linux, CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB sandboxes every command, including shell-mode commands.
- The 84% figure is 'in our internal usage' with no methodology. sandbox-runtime now lives at anthropics/sandbox-runtime.
checks.evidence: The docs say 'The sandbox covers shell commands only.' They list command hooks, local MCP servers, plugin monitors, LSP servers, the status line and apiKeyHelper as running 'with your full access'. They also document the dangerouslyDisableSandbox retry, say docker is incompatible, warn about domain fronting, and state that TLS is not inspected by default. They add that 'Stronger TLS-aware network isolation is an active area of development.' The engineering post is dated 2025-10-20.

checks.claim: Codex demoted Landlock to legacy and defaults to bubblewrap because kernel versions vary across users, and owning the OS image closes that gap.
checks.corrected_statement: The Codex README makes bubblewrap the default and keeps 'the legacy Landlock filesystem implementation'. It gives one reason: Landlock is rejected for filesystem-restricted policies 'because it cannot isolate app-server Unix sockets'. It does not mention kernel-version variance. Pathname Unix socket control arrived in Landlock ABI 9 (Linux 7.1). An OS image could address the stated reason, but only with a floor of 7.1 or later, not 6.15.
checks.evidence: The README states 'Bubblewrap is the default filesystem sandbox.' The OpenAI sandboxing page confirms bwrap on Linux, the Ubuntu 24.04 user-namespace warning (with the bwrap-userns-restrict profile), Seatbelt on macOS and a native Windows sandbox. It does not mention Landlock or seccomp.

checks.claim: On the M1 Pro, the Asahi GPU driver is outside mainline and the Neural Engine driver is out of tree. M3 support arrived 2026-09-06, so Asahi now covers M1 to M3.
checks.corrected_statement:
The M1 Pro facts are confirmed: the GPU and DCP rows say linux-asahi, and the ANE row says out of tree. The Linux 7.2 report (2026-08-26) says GPU and DCP work 'cannot' be upstreamed yet. M3 support (2026-09-06) is official but limited:
- No performant GPU acceleration.
- Sleep does not work.
- HDMI is disabled.
- The M3 Ultra is unsupported.
'Covers M1 to M3' overstates the case for GPU or local-model work.
checks.evidence: The feature table has no update date. The M3 post warns 'Do not expect performant or power-efficient 3D acceleration right now.' The Mesa upstreaming in August 2025 is confirmed (Linux 6.16 report, 2025-08-07).

missed_counter_evidence:
systemd has moved past v258 to v262 (2026-09-22). These releases add features relevant to the 'agent principal as transient unit' design:
- v262: Varlink StartTransient accepts sandboxing, credential and namespace properties.
- v261: RestrictFileSystemAccess= (BPF LSM, dm-verity-only exec) and nspawn RestrictAddressFamilies=.
- v260: mstack, OCI image pull, and FirewallMark= for resolved delegates.
The 'v258 or later' recommendation and the 'no egress features' caveat are stale.

The Landlock ABI-to-kernel mapping (7.0 TSYNC, 7.1 pathname Unix sockets, 7.2 UDP, 7.3-rc ABI 11) invalidates the 6.15 kernel floor. It also shows that the reason Codex gives for treating Landlock as legacy (Unix socket isolation) is addressable on 7.1 or later.
AIOS v0.3.0 (January 2026) and commits through July 2026 weaken the contrarian claim that the flagship agent OS is stagnant.

sandbox-runtime's Windows alpha already uses a dedicated sandbox user account and a WFP egress fence. A userland vendor tool is moving toward per-agent OS identity, which narrows the 'agent principal' moat.

Claude Code has added strictAllowlist, failIfUnavailable, tlsTerminate with credential masking, and SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB full sandboxing. Vendors are closing gaps the brief attributes to the lack of OS ownership.
gpu_ext was evaluated mainly on a consumer RTX 5090, not datacenter GPUs. This contradicts the trend claim and matters for an x86 NVIDIA target.
Adoption figures have moved: Kubernetes agent-sandbox is at v1.0.7 (2026-10-15), not v1.0.2. AgentFS's latest release is v0.6.4 (2026-03-25).
verify:os_level_primitives.reliability_note: I checked primary sources directly: kernel source tags, GitHub API, vendor docs and the Asahi blog. The shared web-search budget ran out before my first search, so I fetched these sources by URL instead. Three areas remain unverified: whether Windows ODR has reached general availability, new 'AI OS' distributions launched in 2026, and newer Codex sandbox changes. Most of the brief's factual claims hold. The three most consequential errors are AIOS's release status, the Landlock kernel floor, and the M3 support scope. The founder should raise the kernel floor to 7.2 or later before relying on Landlock UDP or TSYNC. Two clarifying questions remain: will the image track mainline 7.x kernels, given Asahi's out-of-tree GPU driver? Is UDP or Unix-socket confinement actually required for the first threat model?

checks.claim: Nested virtualization requires Apple M3 or later (macOS 15+), so KVM-based agent sandboxes (Firecracker, Kata, microVM-per-agent) can be tested on the M1 Pro only on bare-metal Asahi or x86 cloud.
checks.corrected_statement: Hardware-accelerated nested virtualization (Virtualization.framework, krunkit, QEMU with HVF) requires M3 or later and macOS 15+, so the M1 Pro cannot run it. A KVM-in-guest stack can still be tested functionally, but very slowly, under QEMU TCG with '-machine virt,virtualization=on'. Realistic sandbox tests need bare-metal Asahi (KVM) or x86 KVM on GitHub x64 runners, where /dev/kvm must first be enabled with a udev rule. GitHub macOS arm64 runners are M1 machines and also lack nested virtualization.
checks.evidence: Apple's documentation for VZGenericPlatformConfiguration.isNestedVirtualizationSupported (macOS 15.0) states that nested virtualization 'is available for Mac with the M3 chip, and later.' The Lima default.yaml says it is supported with vz or krunkit 'on Apple M3 or later (macOS 15 or later)', and with QEMU-HVF only on QEMU 11.1+ on M3+. The QEMU virt documentation describes 'virtualization=on' as emulating the Arm Virtualization Extensions, and its GIC notes tie this option to TCG. TCG emulation is therefore possible but slow, so the claim that this testing is impossible in a VM is overstated. The GitHub changelog of 2024-04-02 confirms KVM on Linux x64 runners (udev rule 99-kvm4all.rules). The GitHub runner reference lists macOS arm64 runners as M1 with 3 CPU and 7 GB and notes 'Nested-virtualization is not supported'. The arm64 Linux runners do not document /dev/kvm.

checks.claim: krunkit/libkrun exposes Vulkan compute only (no rendering) via Venus and MoltenVK at 74-80% of native Metal, so a VM on macOS can beat bare-metal Asahi for LLM work.
checks.corrected_statement: Red Hat measured 74-80% of native Metal overall throughput (RamaLama 0.9.0, llama3.2:1b to llama2:13b) on an M4 Pro with 48 GB under macOS 15.5. Native MoltenVK Vulkan on the host already reached 75-77% of Metal, so most of the loss comes from Vulkan-to-Metal translation, not from virtualization. The path is compute only and is confirmed to work on an M1 Pro. The comparison with Asahi does not use like metrics. On a base M1, Asahi token generation is 88% of Metal (12.47/14.15), which beats the krunkit ratio, so the VM wins there only on prompt processing. On Pro-class chips the VM probably wins on both metrics (see the next check). The 8 GB GPU memory cap from 2024 remains unconfirmed either way.
checks.evidence: The Red Hat article (2025-06-05) reports 20.84 t/s for llama3.1:8b, 'between 74% and 80% of the Metal performance', and states that native ggml-vulkan 'performs at 77%' of ggml-metal. Its metric is overall throughput including TTFT, not pp512/tg128. The Podman Desktop GPU docs say the path 'only supports vulkan compute shaders, not rendering / draw', and the example device is 'Virtio-GPU Venus (Apple M1 Pro)'. The Lima krunkit page says '"krunkit" is experimental' and requires Lima >= 2.0 and macOS >= 14, while its caveats section says Ventura, which contradicts itself. The 2024 sinrega post called the 8 GB cap 'a temporary hard limitation'. The current libkrun README states no cap and warns that the libkrun 2.0 main-branch API 'may change further before the first stable release'.

checks.claim: On Asahi, llama.cpp Vulkan prompt processing is about 3x slower and token generation about 12% slower than Metal on macOS (pp512 38.29/tg128 12.47 vs 117.96/14.15, base M1).
checks.corrected_statement: The base-M1 figures are quoted correctly, but they pair an undated 2025 Vulkan commit with a Metal build from November 2023 (b1550), and they understate the gap on Pro-class chips. On an M2 Pro, Asahi Vulkan reaches pp512 62.70 and tg128 20.95, against 294-341 and 37.9-38.9 on Metal in 2023. That is about 5x slower prompt processing and about 46% slower generation. Current Metal builds are 20-33% faster still. For an M1 Pro (200 GB/s), expect Asahi prompt processing to be roughly 5-6x slower and generation roughly 45-60% slower than current Metal. This is an extrapolation and needs a direct measurement.
checks.evidence: The llama.cpp Vulkan scoreboard (#10879) has these Asahi rows, all without dates and without a Mesa version: M1 38.29/12.47 (commit 2370665), M2 Pro 62.70/20.95, M2 Ultra 205.98/34.34. On 2025-01-14 a maintainer commented: 'I think this is slow on the HoneyKrisp side rather than llama.cpp'. Discussion #4167 (commit 8e672ef, 2023-11-21) lists M1 8c at 117.96/14.15, M1 Pro 16c at 266.25/36.41, and M2 Pro 16c/19c at 294.24-341.19 / 37.87-38.86. A re-run of the M2 Ultra 76c at commit c1d0e7a (2026-08-25) shows 1488.81/125.21, against 1238.48/94.27 in 2023. No M1 Pro row exists for Asahi.

checks.claim: Public GitHub repos get free x64 runners with KVM and free arm64 runners; GPU runners (T4, $0.052/min) require a Team or Enterprise plan, are always charged, and cannot boot a custom OS.
checks.corrected_statement: These points are confirmed: free standard runners for public repositories (x64 and arm64, 4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 14 GB SSD), KVM on Linux x64 via a udev rule, a GPU runner at $0.052/min ($3.12/hr) with a T4 (16 GB VRAM, 4 vCPU, 28 GB RAM, 176 GB SSD), and larger runners always charged, even for public repositories. These points are not confirmed: current documentation does not name a Team or Enterprise plan requirement (it requires a payment method and a spending limit above $0, set up at organization or enterprise level), and /dev/kvm on arm64 runners is undocumented. The claim 'cannot boot a custom OS' is overstated. Larger runners support custom images for Linux x64, Linux ARM64 and Windows x64 that can start from 'a clean OS'. GPU support for custom images is undocumented, and these images are still runner VMs, not arbitrary bootloader tests.
checks.evidence: The Actions runner pricing page lists linux_4_core_gpu at $0.052, actions_linux at $0.006 and actions_linux_arm at $0.005 per minute. The billing concepts page says 'Larger runners are always charged for, even when used by public repositories'. The larger-runners reference names Enterprise Cloud only for static IP addresses. The custom images how-to says images can start from 'a clean OS' on Linux x64, Linux ARM64 and Windows x64. The runner reference now also lists ubuntu-26.04 and ubuntu-26.04-arm labels.

checks.claim: Asahi status: Fedora Asahi Remix 43 shipped 18 March 2026 and FAR 44 was targeted for 28 April 2026; the 21,000-line GPU kernel driver is still downstream (upstreaming began February 2026); M3 support entered the installer in September 2026; the GPU lead left in August 2025; Thunderbolt and DP Alt Mode remain WIP on M1 Pro.
checks.corrected_statement: All parts are confirmed, with updates. FAR 44 has since shipped: asahilinux.org/fedora now says the remix is 'based on Fedora Linux 44', although the exact release date was not verified. The M3 post is titled 'M2: Episode 1 (or, Asahi Linux on M3)', and an update dated 2026-09-15 removed the Expert-mode requirement. The Thunderbolt progress in the 7.2 report applies to M3, not M1, so M1 Pro Thunderbolt and DP Alt Mode are still WIP. The claim that the team has moved away from M1 polish is weak: the April 2026 report added PMP idle-power work for the 14-inch M1 Pro, and FAR 43 added 120 Hz support for the MacBook Pro 14/16.
checks.evidence: Fedora Magazine published the FAR 43 article on 2026-03-18. The 7.0 report (2026-04-26) says the team was 'still on track to release Fedora Asahi Remix 44 either on or within a few days of Fedora Linux 44 on 28 April'. The 6.19 report (2026-02-15) says 'The GPU driver is 21,000 lines by itself' and that upstreaming 'has now begun'; it also reports patches falling from 1232 to 858 and lines from 95,000 to 83,000. The 7.1 report (2026-06-30) says GPU initialisation moved into m1n1 ahead of LKML submission. The 7.2 report (2026-08-26) mentions 'enormous work that we cannot upstream yet (e.g. GPU, DCP)'. Rosenzweig wrote on 2025-08-26: 'I am now stepping away from the Apple ecosystem'; her post says the Mesa drivers are upstream and lists Vulkan 1.4 and OpenCL 3.0 conformance. The M1 feature page lists Thunderbolt WIP, DP Alt Mode WIP, video encode TBA, Touch ID TBA and ANE out of tree.

missed_counter_evidence: The Asahi speed gap is much larger on Pro-class chips than on the base M1. An M2 Pro on Asahi reaches tg128 20.95 against about 38 on Metal, so 'about 12% slower generation' should not be used to plan for an M1 Pro.

Ollama's MLX engine launched in preview on 30 March 2026 and required 'a Mac with more than 32 GB unified memory'. The June 2026 update gives no guidance for 16 GB machines. The 'Ollama moved to MLX' trend therefore does little for a 16 GB M1 Pro, where mlx-lm or llama.cpp Metal remain the practical paths.

Red Hat's own data shows native MoltenVK Vulkan reaching only 75-77% of Metal on the host. The krunkit penalty is therefore mostly translation overhead, so KosmicKrisp could narrow it. This deserves a direct test rather than relying on the 2025 ratio.

This session's host reports Darwin 27.2 (macOS 27). If that host is the M1 Pro, it already meets the macOS 26 requirement for Apple container and KosmicKrisp, so the brief overstates those limitations. Apple also says Rosetta will be available as a general-purpose tool only 'through macOS 27', so the window for Rosetta-based x86_64 userspace testing on the Mac is about one year.
QEMU TCG with virtualization=on can emulate EL2. Nested KVM is therefore possible on the M1, but only for slow functional smoke tests.

GitHub larger runners support custom images that can start from 'a clean OS' (Linux x64 and ARM64). Whether GPU runners accept them is undocumented. This weakens the absolute claim that they 'cannot boot a custom OS'.

GitHub has added ubuntu-26.04 and ubuntu-26.04-arm runner labels. The actions/partner-runner-images repository, which supplied the arm64 images, was archived in June 2026. Whether arm64 runners expose /dev/kvm is still undocumented and should be checked with a CI step.

Asahi 7.1 (June 2026) moved GPU initialisation into m1n1 to prepare the driver for LKML submission. Asahi 7.2 reports DCP nearly at parity with the macOS 13.5 ABI. A new AVD V4L2 decode driver exists but is not shipped by default in FAR.
The Asahi 7.0 PMP saving (about 0.5 W on a 14-inch M1 Pro) is disabled by default, and base M1 machines use an incompatible PMP variant.

On 13 October 2026, Ollama and Fly.io launched Sprites, persistent sandboxed Linux VMs for AI agents in the cloud. Established vendors now market VM-per-agent isolation, which weakens the novelty claim behind the 'microVM per agent' opportunity, although no AgentOS-style distribution was found.

The '66.7% default GPU share' comes from a 2023 community code snippet in llama.cpp discussion #2182, not from Apple documentation. It should be checked on the M1 Pro against llama.cpp's recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize log line.

AWS GPU instance families are subject to per-family vCPU quotas, which may need an increase request before the first g4dn or g6 launch. This was not verified in this pass and should be checked before relying on per-release automation.

Method: the shared WebSearch budget was already used up at the start of this pass (only one search was attempted, and it was refused). All checks therefore rest on about 40 direct fetches of primary pages (Apple, GitHub, Asahi, Fedora Magazine, Lima, QEMU, Red Hat, llama.cpp, Ollama). Some pages showed self-contradictions (Lima's macOS minimum) or undated rows (llama.cpp scoreboard), and the FAR 44 release date was not confirmed. No files were changed. Two questions for the orchestrator: (1) Does the development M1 Pro run macOS 27, as this host reports? (2) Will AgentOS ship Apple Silicon bare-metal images as a supported target, or only use Asahi for development? Each answer changes how much weight the Asahi findings deserve.
